talks.title: The Vulnerability Identity Crisis
talks.teaser: Proposes a structural definition of vulnerabilities built from a system, a weakness, conditions and a violated property.
talks.summary:
Art and Jay describe two years of weekly work on the minimum information a public vulnerability record needs. The effort began with a question about which fields in a CVE record are essential. Their early attempt at a short list of key elements broke down on edge cases, so they gathered 29 definitions from academic papers and frameworks. None of them covered the anomalies they cared about, such as controversial CVE entries, a curl command-line option that only matters inside automation or a CGI deployment, and Linux kernel disputes over flaws that have not shipped yet.

They propose that a vulnerability is not simply a weakness. It is a weakness in a named system, combined with a set of conditions that must all be met before a security property is violated. They use glass as an analogy: it has a tendency to break, but only under specific force applied to a specific spot. They also cite an exploit that needed 16 conditions to be met, and note that disabling or controlling any one of them stops the attack. They argue that confidentiality, integrity and availability hide how serious a flaw is, and prefer describing the principle, action and effect instead. The identifier is compared to a peg, with self-contained assertions hung on it as bags that can be added as evidence emerges.

In the question session, they agreed that misconfigurations and inherently insecure protocols can fit the definition. They also said cryptographic weaknesses, such as MD5 collisions, become vulnerabilities when external conditions change while the system itself stays the same. They closed by saying the terminology is still being refined, drawing on Carnap's method of explication. Their goal is a working definition that practitioners can test against their own records, including adding missing information to existing logs.

talks.title: One Poisoned Artifact Can Steer Your AI: How Robust Are Your LLM-Assisted Security Workflows?
talks.teaser: Shows how one poisoned document can win retrieval and steer a RAG-based security assistant toward malicious commands.
talks.summary:
The talk examines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistants that security teams use to answer questions from internal wikis, threat reports and logs. Using a recent supply-chain compromise of a popular LLM package as the running example, the speakers argue that anyone able to edit the knowledge base can slip in content the assistant will trust.

The attack hides two parts in one planted document: retrieval bait that makes the retriever rank it highly for the target query, and instructions aimed at the generator that steer the analyst toward an attacker-controlled command. Both parts are tuned with the GCG discrete optimization method to pull model attention onto chosen strings. In a test over 500 documents, the average retrieval rank was 15 before optimization and the attack success rate was 18%. Improving retrieval moved the average rank to second, and improving the generator raised success to 86%, for an overall increase of 68%. A live demo showed a normal answer before the attack and a recommendation to run a malicious command after it.

Suggested defenses include treating random-looking strings and malformed markup in retrieved text as a warning sign, scanning the retrieval pipeline with protection models or filters, and flagging retrieved documents whose meaning contradicts the rest of the set. The key takeaway is that a single malicious element can be enough to manipulate an AI-assisted workflow.

talks.title: Attack or Noise?: Tracking and Evaluating the Impact of Internet-Wide Survey Scanners
talks.teaser: Defenders learn darknet attribution of internet-wide scanners and SIEM use of maintained inventories to cut firewall and IDS noise.
talks.summary:
Internet-facing networks are probed constantly by measurement vendors, researchers, and opaque actors whose traffic is not necessarily malicious but still floods security operations. The presenters describe how Japan’s NICT uses long-running darknet sinks—hundreds of thousands of unused addresses—to separate bot-driven victim hunting from survey-like scanning, then validate candidates through reverse DNS, banner grabs, open sources, and honeypot payloads.

Over a 90-day window in the first quarter of 2026 they logged 221.5 billion darknet packets, with identified and unknown survey scanners accounting for 67.5% of observations while malware-style bots formed a smaller share. They attributed scans from 83 organizations, characterized persistence and port coverage for major services such as Modat, Censys, Shadowserver, and Shodan, and highlighted cloud-hosted infrastructure that complicates ownership. Unknown scanners especially require honeypot follow-up because behavior ranges from benign HTTP probes to hostile traversal attempts.

The SOC-focused segment quantifies operational pain: roughly 32% of inbound firewall records and more than 40% of IDS alerts traced to known scanners, plus on the order of 100 gigabytes per day of log storage. Integrating a maintained scanner inventory into the SIEM enables lookups, respects different firewall versus IDS signatures, and exploits periodic scan schedules where they exist. The closing recommendations urge scanner operators to identify themselves and offer opt-outs, while defenders share attribution metadata through community inventories instead of rebuilding lists in isolation.

talks.title: Proactive EDR Against Adaptive Evasion: Countering Self‑Modifying Agentic Malware
talks.teaser: Shows how AI-driven malware evades endpoint tools and proposes detection pillars that watch behavior patterns instead of binaries.
talks.summary:
The talk examines malware that embeds a language model as its own decision engine, rewriting its commands at runtime rather than relying on fixed signatures or a remote command server. Drawing on a threat report about AI-enabled malware families, the speaker models three proof-of-concept scenarios in an isolated lab. In the first, a Python script using only standard libraries asks an external API for each next stage, running generated code in memory across reconnaissance, encryption, data staging and self-deletion. The rhythm of API calls, paced by model response time, is the detectable signal.

The second scenario switches inference to a model hosted on a local port, so traffic never leaves the host and network-based command-and-control detection loses visibility. The third poisons the Markdown context file that a coding agent loads at session start, so the agent carries out the injected instructions under its own trusted identity. The file modification and the agent's activity are the only traces. Testing covered Windows Defender with enhanced settings on a single host; enterprise EDR products were not evaluated.

The core problem is that these actions look like legitimate AI workflows at the telemetry level, so blocking by indicator or process name fails. The proposed response has three pillars: sequence monitoring of interpreter-to-API behaviour and timing, binding and monitoring local model API calls, and integrity monitoring of agent context files. Wider measures include routing API calls through a gateway, logging prompts locally and version-controlling context files. Practitioners should inventory AI tools, review agent context files and confirm that AI-related traffic is monitored.

talks.title: My CERT PL - Free Security Tools for Everyone (in Poland)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in My CERT PL - Free Security Tools for Everyone (in Poland).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Krzysztof Zając from CERT Polska (one of Poland's three national-level CERTs, responsible for private entities and the general public) presents **mojecert.pl** (My CERT PL). The initiative is a free security portal designed to help organizations, small businesses, and individuals assess and strengthen their cybersecurity posture. The platform addresses several recurring challenges faced by national CERTs: cyber incidents stemming from unpatched vulnerabilities or leaked credentials (such as an attack on the Polish Press Agency used to publish fake mobilization news), difficulty communicating available security tools to the public, limited visibility into non-governmental infrastructure, and fragmented or outdated organizational contact information.

### Key Topics
- **Target Audience and Motivation**: Providing free scanning and threat notifications to everyone—ranging from personal blog owners to large enterprises—especially entities lacking substantial cybersecurity budgets.
- **Domain & Subnet Onboarding**: Users register infrastructure assets. Domain ownership is verified via DNS TXT records or file placement on the web server; subnet verification is handled manually via ISP confirmation or RIPE database records to prevent unauthorized scanning.
- **Core Services Offered**: Automated vulnerability scanning, leaked credential notifications, network event monitoring, security advisories, fishing protection verification, and email spoofing diagnostics.
- **Ecosystem Collaboration**: Sharing dashboards and threat data with sectoral CERTs (such as the Polish financial sector CERT and health sector CERT) and integrating European NIS2 directive requirements.
- **Architecture and Development Philosophy**: Building rapidly using open-source utilities and "boring," dependable technologies rather than complex frameworks.

### Technical Details
- **Security Scanning (Artemis)**: Scanning is powered by CERT Polska's open-source tool Artemis, which orchestrates modular scans utilizing established open-source tools like Nuclei and SQLMap. Artemis runs dozens of modules to identify issues ranging from outdated WordPress versions and misconfigured email security (SPF/DMARC) to severe flaws like SQL injection and remote code execution.
- **Network Event Aggregation (N6)**: CERT Polska's open-source N6 aggregator ingests data from more than 90 sources (notably Shadowserver) to track malicious activity such as malware command-and-control communication, infected hosts (e.g., SmokeLoader), and scanning activity. Mojecert.pl enriches this telemetry with accessible explanations.
- **Credential Leak Monitoring**: Ingests password dumps from public releases, internal threat hunting, commercial providers, and stealer malware logs to alert affected email providers and website administrators.
- **Phishing Defense Verification & MailGoose**: Allows administrators to test whether local networks are protected by the CERT Polska warning list, a DNS-level blocklist that blocked 141 million malicious page views in 2025. It also integrates MailGoose, an open-source tool for validating SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configurations.
- **Tech Stack & Operations**: Developed with Django, PostgreSQL, and Kubernetes without complex single-page JavaScript frameworks. Scans repeat cyclically (defaulting to every two months), managed by a team that expanded from two to six developers.

### Takeaways
- **Rapid, Pragmatic Deployment**: Starting small with a basic beta after five months proved successful; projects do not need polished graphic design or extensive feature sets upfront to deliver immediate value.
- **Opt-in Legal Foundation**: By having users register and give explicit consent to be scanned, CERTs, hosting providers, or NGOs do not require prior government mandate or broad statutory scanning authority.
- **Demonstrated Impact**: Mojecert.pl has grown to over 20,000 users and 24,000 verified domains, uncovering hundreds of thousands of vulnerabilities. Future planned capabilities include on-boarding additional sectoral CERTs and a privacy-preserving file reputation check to assess malware without leaking sensitive data to public repositories.

talks.title: Beyond Manual Hunting: OSINT Copilot with LLMs & Evidence-Based Collection, Enrichment ...
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Beyond Manual Hunting: OSINT Copilot with LLMs & Evidence-Based Collection, Enrichment ....
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Victor and Matos, this talk examines the intersection of cybersecurity threat research and data engineering. The speakers address the primary bottleneck facing threat analysts: sifting through massive volumes of raw, noisy data from forums, marketplaces, and other sources to produce actionable intelligence for decision-makers. Rather than relying solely on manual hunting or external proprietary LLMs, the speakers propose an end-to-end pipeline that combines distributed data collection, deterministic entity extraction, local small language model (SLM) semantic enrichment, vector search, and agent-driven contextual investigation.

### Key Topics
- **Hunting Challenges & Pipeline Philosophy**: Threat research requires moving beyond raw data collection to actionable intelligence. The speakers emphasize that "data engineering comes first" and "the pipeline is the product"—language models alone cannot fix unstructured or unorganized data.
- **Data Collection Trade-Offs**: Gathering data from diverse sources involves choosing between lightweight HTTP clients (scalable and low resource, but unable to execute JavaScript or manage browser footprints) and browser automation (handles JavaScript, bypasses barriers, and manages device fingerprints, but incurs heavy resource and complexity overhead).
- **Dual-Layer Enrichment**: Processing unstructured post text requires both deterministic extraction (regex/pattern parsing for IPs, emails, domains, URLs, and cryptocurrency wallets) and semantic analysis via language models (identifying intent, company mentions, communication context, and risk/revenue tags).
- **Local/Small Language Models vs. Commercial APIs**: Processing millions of events and billions of tokens daily makes external APIs (such as Entropic or Openi) cost-prohibitive. The team deploys self-hosted smaller models using optimization tools such as VLM (for GPU KV cache management) and MTP (multi-token prediction) to guarantee privacy, predictable costs, and steady output.

### Technical Details
- **Extraction & Normalization**: Data pipelines handle session management, fingerprint rotation, and deduplication. Collected posts are parsed into metadata fields (forum name, topic ID, post ID, creation date, collection date, language, raw text).
- **Embedding & Search Architecture**: Enrichment generates event summaries, risk indicators, and vector embeddings. Embeddings are stored in a dedicated index separate from original documents to prevent data loss. Documents are indexed in a distributed search engine (referenced as Galaxy/logical search engine) supporting both BM25 keyword matching and vector similarity.
- **Contextual Graph & Agentic Investigation**: When an analyst queries an entity (e.g., an actor name like Gordon Freeman), hundreds or thousands of matching events may appear. To make this manageable, an AI agent equipped with database access tools navigates the schema, groups relevant fields, and constructs connection graphs across multiple sources. In an illustrated case study, this approach linked actors ("Cipher 403", "Home Home Hoot One") and a threat group ("F") targeting South American countries (Venezuela, Argentina, Guatemala, Chile, Ecuador) and Canada.
- **Benchmarking**: Tests across more than 10,000 events demonstrated that smaller local models performed comparably to large frontier models for risk indexing and entity dimensions, with only slight differences observed in text summarization.

### Takeaways
- Language models cannot compensate for poor data engineering; structured collection, parsing, and normalization must precede AI integration.
- Self-hosted smaller models running in-cluster provide superior data privacy, latency control, and cost predictability for high-volume threat data processing.
- Combining deterministic indicators with semantic risk tags allows automated filtering, enabling analysts and investigative agents to focus exclusively on high-priority events and relationship mapping.

talks.title: Defeating Node.js Malware through API Tracing
talks.teaser: Shows how hooking Node.js APIs reveals what obfuscated malware does and bypasses its anti-analysis checks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that tracing, which records the API calls a program makes as it runs, is a useful first step in malware analysis, because it cuts through heavy obfuscation without needing breakpoints or prior knowledge of the code. The speaker also outlines a typical Node.js loader: checks on memory, CPU count and processes, a PowerShell call to elevate privileges, then a payload fetched from a server and launched.

The speaker's Node.js tracer hooks the module loader so that every function in a loaded module gets wrapped. Analysts can log calls, return spoofed values to pass checks such as RAM size, CPU count and process lists, skip sleep calls and save dropped files. In a demo on a loader sample, the trace showed the checks being passed, attempts to kill Windows Defender, a lock file being created and two command-and-control hosts being contacted. Feeding the trace to an LLM with a short prompt produced a markdown report with indicators. In another case, about 300 samples from one campaign were run in parallel to recover their next-stage payloads.

The main takeaways are that obfuscation cannot hide runtime behaviour, and that bypasses for common anti-analysis checks can be reused across samples. Limits include no view of the logic between API calls and no source recovery, and system-level monitoring misses checks that happen inside the Node.js runtime. The tool is open source, and the speaker expects an arms race, since attackers could eventually unhook.

talks.title: Itinerary to Defeat Yet Another Beacon Implementation
talks.teaser: Shows how to extract config and apply FLIRT signatures to Cobalt Strike beacon reimplementations written in Rust and Go.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Cobalt Strike's beacon payload, the implant used after initial access, and at how it is being rebuilt in modern languages. It begins with the framework's abuse by state-linked groups and cybercrime, including a cluster tied to APT27 and the Black Basta ransomware gang. Custom beacons, and loaders that only run in specific Active Directory environments, can defeat common configuration extractors and detection rules, which makes independent Rust and Go implementations harder to triage.

Three open-source projects are examined in turn. The first, a Rust project from 2023 that is no longer maintained, implements only a few commands and stores its configuration in plain text, so the strings output exposes the C2 address, although Rust string slices can add a stray trailing character. The second, a richer Rust implementation from 2024, builds its C2 URL at runtime, so an analyst has to trace the formatting structure to locate it. The third, the Go-based GeaconPro, was taken private by its original author, but public copies remain. Its configuration is initialized in a single function, and more than 100 VirusTotal samples with differing C2 addresses were found.

For reverse engineering, each project was built as a static library so that FLIRT signatures could be generated and applied to stripped binaries, labeling library functions and making the C2 communication routines easier to find. Signature files for builds made with Rust 1.92.0 and Go 1.26.1, along with YARA rules, were published. The main takeaway is that open-source implementations expose configuration in readable form, but attackers can add obfuscation, so signatures and binary diffing remain useful fallbacks.

talks.title: Introducing StealerLens: An LLM-Powered Forensics Microscope to Accelerate InfoStealer ...
talks.teaser: Shows how an LLM pipeline filters infostealer log artifacts to hypothesize how a victim was infected.
talks.summary:
Infostealer malware quietly collects passwords, cookies, browser history and files from an infected machine, and the results are sold as zipped stealer logs on Telegram and criminal forums. Each bundle keeps artifacts such as system details, clipboard contents, screenshots and installed software lists separate. A typical log is several megabytes across dozens of files, which makes manual review slow for responders trying to find how the infection began.

The presenters describe StealerLens, which uses one prompt per artifact because a single prompt covering everything failed. Browsing history is trimmed to the days before infection to fit model context limits, reputable and benign domains are dropped, and file-sharing sites are flagged. Repeated processes are counted instead of listed, and static advertisement screenshots are removed with perceptual hashing. Structured outputs keep results consistent, and a final prompt asks for an infection hypothesis with supporting evidence. A demo pointed to a cracked Adobe Lightroom download as the likely vector. Early tests on 25 logs gave good results for 21; the other four needed extra handling for ClickFix, AutoIt and missing evidence.

Most vectors seen were cracked software, though GitHub, YouTube and ClickFix lures also appeared. The speaker warned that a model primed with known patterns may miss genuinely new techniques. Analysis takes one to three minutes per log, and the tool automates filtering so analysts keep the judgement. Access is limited to verified practitioners because the data is sensitive.

talks.title: Understanding Scammer Threats: Detection Strategies Aligned with Thailand’s Cybersecurity Act 2562
talks.teaser: Maps Thailand's scam landscape and the national response, from SIM rules and bank freezes to ad verification duties.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at scam operations in Thailand, which the speaker describes as highly organized transnational crime linked to human trafficking and money laundering. It presents national figures on mobile and internet use and on reported scam losses, then explains how the national reporting line and anti-scam center coordinate rapid bank account suspension, refunds and data sharing between police, banking and telecom regulators.

The speaker walks through a typical scam sequence: first contact by phone, SMS or social media, a lure to a fake investment, shopping or government site, and then a fake app that collects credentials, controls the phone and overlays the screen to move money. The countermeasures described include limits on SIM registration, locating SIM boxes that route overseas calls, blocking links in bank and government SMS, reverse engineering a malicious app to find its command servers, and changing biometric checks to require random movements and disabling remote-control features in banking apps.

The legal section covers a 2023 royal decree on cybercrime prevention, its 2025 revision that speeds refunds and adds duties for financial institutions and digital asset operators, and a new rule requiring identity verification and 90-day ad data retention for platforms that sell advertising. The main takeaway is that the approach combines public awareness, telecom rules, bank controls and legislation, and the speaker noted that the platform rule was not yet in effect at the time.

talks.title: Building a Regional ISAC for West Africa that Works: Governance, Tools and Community Maturity
talks.teaser: Describes building a regional information sharing centre for West African response teams, and the governance hurdles met.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a regional information sharing and analysis centre can be set up for the twelve member states of the Economic Community of West African States. The speakers start by untangling team terminology, placing CSIRTs, SOCs, PSIRTs and ISACs against the FIRST service framework, and explain that an ISAC focuses on situational awareness and advice rather than hands-on incident handling. They then describe why national teams differ widely in size, and why an earlier European regional incident team, launched around 1997, failed, mainly because very few incidents were reported. Governments were reluctant to share information, so the project had to win formal authorisation, write a charter, and prepare a memorandum of understanding that needs ministerial signatures.

Practical steps included several in-person meetings with realistic scenario exercises, a dedicated MISP platform for distributing information, and rotating volunteers to lead the information management system for short periods. The speakers' lessons were that clear terminology shapes expectations, that trust depends on face-to-face contact with named people, that processes should be kept simple so they do not block sharing, and that participants should be given real responsibility so outside experts can step back. They stressed that the model is still being finalised, and that success should be judged through indicators defined for each individual service.

talks.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once…in 2038
talks.teaser: Explains how 2038 Unix time rollovers could break systems, and how researchers measured exposure across NTP, SNMP, TVs and more.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the 2038 rollover, when 32-bit signed Unix time counters run out and wrap back to the past, and the earlier NTP rollover due in 2036. The speaker notes that a fix for NTP has been in the stable ntpd branch since 2014, yet around 40% of observed servers still report vulnerable versions. Because NTP is treated as a trusted time source, a wrong upstream clock spreads downstream, and about 39% of roughly 2.5 million clients were seen speaking NTP version three, which can roll over regardless of the server.

Measurement followed across several sources. An NTP scan found about 123,000 servers, around 50,000 of which would roll over in 2038. Of roughly 15 million SNMP responses, about 600K reported version data and around 20,000 revealed kernel and architecture details, with about 13,000 of those expected to fail. Two fuel tank gauges from different vendors failed the same way, issuing always-expired authentication tokens. Sinkhole telemetry showed around 127k infected smart TVs in one week, and about 6% of the tested models were expected to crash. Where direct data was missing, Debian popularity statistics suggested around 8% of Debian Apache servers run 32-bit systems.

The talk stresses that scanning is triage, not proof, so systems need real testing. It suggests ranking fixes by harm, putting life safety, medical and emergency communications first, and limiting damage where repair is impossible, for example through simpler designs, human override or graceful degradation. For buyers, it urges certification, escrowed source and builds, and inventories of time dependencies.

talks.teaser: Covers the CVE program, AI software bill of materials, and end-of-support tracking for edge devices in this interview.
talks.summary:
This First Impressions podcast interview, recorded at the FIRST conference in Denver, has an acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity at CISA describing the agency's mission. CISA defends federal civilian agencies, state, local, tribal and territorial governments, and US critical infrastructure. The conversation centres on the CVE program, which the agency helps operate as a shared public resource. The official says the numbering authority federation has grown from about 26 to more than 500 over roughly a decade, and that 48,000 records were published last year with a pace to exceed that this year.

The discussion then turns to supply chain risk. Software bill of materials minimum elements, along with best-practice guidance for publishing them, help organizations check quickly whether they run a compromised version of a product. Open source package manager compromises show why CVEs should be registered for malicious packages as well. A G7 effort builds on those minimum elements for AI systems, adding AI-specific items such as model information and versions. The agency is also working with vendors to publish machine-readable end-of-support timelines using OpenEOX, so unsupported network and edge equipment can be identified during scanning.

The interview closes on staffing. The official describes a hiring sprint that expects about 180 temporary job offers within a month, and explains that movement between industry and government gives both sides useful experience. The practical takeaway is that inventory gaps, especially at the network edge, weaken both vulnerability scanning and supply chain response.

talks.title: Episode 58: Cheng-Lin Yang and Lily Chen, CyCraft, FIRSTCON26 Speakers
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Episode 58: Cheng-Lin Yang and Lily Chen, CyCraft, FIRSTCON26 Speakers.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this episode of the First Impressions podcast, hosts Christian Riley and Martin McKay speak with CyCraft researchers Liddy Chen (Data Scientist) and George Yang (Data Scientist Director) about their upcoming FIRSTCON26 presentation, "One Poisoned Artifact Can Steer Your AI: How Robust Are Your LLM Assisted Security Workflows?" The talk explores the vulnerabilities that arise when security analysts rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to browse the web and summarize incident reports, showing how an attacker can manipulate LLM-assisted workflows by placing a single crafted document online.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of AI Manipulation:** While earlier models could be tricked by simple social engineering or emotional prompts, modern LLMs feature higher baseline safety. Attackers must now focus on attention mechanisms to bias output generation.
- **Indirect Prompt Injection:** Rather than sending prompts directly to the model, an attacker creates an external, poisoned document designed to catch the LLM's attention during external searches and alter its conclusions.
- **Attack-Defense Asymmetry:** Modern AI security mirrors traditional cybersecurity "cat-and-mouse" dynamics. Offensive techniques continue to emerge and grow stronger, while generalizable defensive strategies have yet to converge.

### Technical Details
The researchers describe a two-stage attack optimization strategy split across the primary components of retrieval-augmented LLM architectures:
1. **Attracting the Retriever:** One portion of the malicious document is optimized to attract the attention of the model's search/retrieval component, ensuring the document is selected from the web or an input corpus.
2. **Targeting the Generator:** A second portion is designed to influence the text generation component, forcing the LLM to alter its final summary, recommend malicious phishing URLs, or output incorrect claims.

During optimization, these documents often accumulate unnatural artifacts, appearing as gibberish or random-looking strings. Testing also revealed that attacks optimized for a specific model exhibit transferability across different LLMs, with smaller models generally proving easier to compromise. The technical foundations of this work were recently accepted at the ICML AI conference.

### Takeaways
- **Inspect Noisy Artifacts:** Analysts and pipelines should not ignore gibberish strings or abnormal artifacts in raw logs and web content, as they may be optimized payloads designed to trigger model attention.
- **Implement Contradiction Filtering:** Organizations should run secondary filters to detect whether a retrieved document contradicts the consensus of other gathered sources or drifts from the original query context before feeding it into generator models.

talks.title: Beyond Human Scale: AI and Automation as Force Multipliers in Cyber Threat Intelligence
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Beyond Human Scale: AI and Automation as Force Multipliers in Cyber Threat Intelligence.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, members of the AWS Security Incident Response team share lessons learned and architectural methodologies developed while building a hybrid AI security tool for threat intelligence and data analysis. Facing head count constraints when manually analyzing massive volumes of AWS CloudTrail logs across customer security incidents, the team designed a solution that pairs traditional deterministic programming with an AI enhancement layer to extract threat actor actions, reconstruct kill chains, and correlate trends across cases.

### Key Topics
- **Operational Discovery**: Identifying repetitive tasks and clear input boundaries across weekly team workflows to establish an automation roadmap.
- **Consumer vs. Creator Personas**: Shifting from passive consumer AI tasks (such as code generation or summarization) to creating custom AI-enabled systems and pipelines.
- **Threat Technique Catalog for AWS (TTC)**: An AWS-specific extension of the MITRE ATT&CK framework used to categorize and map observed threat actor API calls.
- **Decision Criteria for Automation**: Evaluating factors such as output criticality, downstream impact, accuracy versus throughput, acceptable error tolerances, token costs, and data privacy.

### Technical Details
- **Deterministic Logic Layer**: Raw CloudTrail logs are initially ingested and processed using traditional Python recursive depth-first search (DFS) algorithms with parallel processing. This layer isolates threat actor activity from benign activity deterministically rather than relying directly on an LLM.
- **Graph Transformation & Technique Mapping**: Filtered CloudTrail CSV logs are converted into a graph data structure. Nodes represent individual API calls classified using the Threat Technique Catalog (e.g., initial access, discovery, impact). Paths are traversed from impact actions backward to initial access points.
- **Embedding-Based Pruning and Semantic Ranking**: Candidate paths contain noise and benign operations. The team generates vector embeddings for each API call and computes similarity against the impact action to prune irrelevant or read-only calls. Remaining paths are semantically ranked by relevance.
- **LLM Synthesis & Validation**: Only after thorough programmatic filtering and ranking is an LLM invoked to select and synthesize final kill chains and summaries. Output quality is validated by comparing LLM-generated summaries against documented incident ticket summaries, combined with custom validation models and human-in-the-loop review.
- **Performance**: The hybrid pipeline demonstrated the capability to process roughly 990 million records in under 20 to 25 minutes, identifying shared patterns across hundreds and thousands of customer security cases.

### Takeaways
- **Hybrid Architecture Over Pure AI**: Directly feeding raw logs to LLMs or autonomous agents is cost-prohibitive, slow, and prone to non-deterministic errors that trigger noisy downstream alerts. Deterministic layers provide precision and scale, while AI handles contextual synthesis.
- **Realistic Data Sets**: Models trained purely on synthetic or red team datasets struggled in production because the data was too clean; real-world messy data is vital for handling noise.
- **Trust Determines Adoption**: Incident responders will abandon tools if outputs lack transparency. Explaining tool inputs and high-level logic empowers analysts to trust and validate the results.
- **POC vs. Production Scale**: Prototype designs must account for token costs, infrastructure limits, and system permissions from day one, including conducting threat modeling to restrict tool access.

talks.title: Hunting Cyber Threat Intelligence on Telegram
talks.teaser: Shows how a research team maps cybercriminal Telegram communities by snowballing outward from manually chosen seed channels.
talks.summary:
Luca and Roy, from a Dutch university research group, presented their work on finding and monitoring cybercriminal communities on Telegram. They framed the problem as socio-technical: the platform is vast, noisy and rate-limited, so following every link or forward wastes resources and drifts into channels with no real threat information.

Roy introduced TeleHunt, a tool that starts from analyst-chosen seed communities, scrapes their messages and classifies each one as cybercriminal or not, then assigns a market segment such as attacks, stolen data or fraud tools. It extracts pointers to other communities from handles, links and forwards, and snowballs through them, using the context around each pointer to stay on track. In a test run, configurations that followed links found the most communities with stable precision, while those without links stalled. Invite links expire on administrator-set schedules, so late extraction produced dead ends. Rediscovery was very low, suggesting the ecosystem was far from saturated.

Luca described Television, an in-progress analysis toolset, in which communities linked by referrals formed clusters and bridging nodes without manual grouping. Early results pointed to Russian-speaking communities discussing bulletproof hosting linked to Iranian hacktivist spaces. The collected data is being built into a queryable knowledge graph. The takeaways were to start from seeds that matter, treat forums and Telegram as connected rather than separate, and expect a large, fragmented ecosystem.

talks.title: OpenTide: From Raw Intelligence to Structured Threat-Informed Detections
talks.teaser: Explores an open-source framework that turns raw threat intelligence into deployable detection rules across multiple security platforms.
talks.summary:
European Commission detection engineers describe a growing operational gap: threat intelligence arrives faster than teams can translate it into validated rules for SIEM and EDR platforms. Manual report review, TTP extraction, and rule authoring remain the bottleneck, and MITRE ATT&CK alone lacks the behavioral granularity, risk context, and chaining detection engineers need for prioritization and coverage.

OpenTide (presented as Open Threat in the session) is a schema-driven, Git-native framework linking threat vectors, detection objectives, signals, and deployable rules. It models threat surfaces against organizational assets and log availability, supports multi-tenant deployment to vendors such as Sentinel, Defender, Splunk, and CrowdStrike, and encodes detection-as-code through CI/CD. Agent Tide layers coding agents on the same schemas to turn unstructured intel (including long reports or linked articles) into validated objects in roughly fifteen minutes, using parallel sub-agents and human-style review patterns.

Practitioners gain a repeatable intel-to-detection lifecycle with coverage tracing—objectives with signals lacking data or rules—and an EU-licensed open stack already used in production for more than two years, with shared threat vectors and emerging query-language skills for generated rules.

talks.title: CTI-Transmute: Harmonizing Threat Intelligence in a Multi-Standard Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Introduces an open-source conversion service that translates between MISP and STIX so tools need not implement either format.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces CTI Transmute, an open-source conversion layer with an online service that translates threat intelligence between MISP and STIX. The presenters explain that the project started when developers of the AIL analysis framework were asked to add STIX support and did not want to maintain conversion code inside their own tool. Instead, conversion is handled by a separate service that other tools can call through a simple API.

The middle of the talk covers how conversion works and where it gets difficult. The core relies on the MISP-STIX Python library, which handles STIX 1.2 and MISP, and mappings are chosen to preserve analyst intent, since fields can share names yet carry different meanings. Bidirectional conversion has to avoid losing data, for example with custom vendor extensions and with MISP's single IDS flag, which STIX splits across separate data elements. The speakers said that few users exercise the full STIX pattern language, with usage around 5 to 10 percent of its scope, so full coverage is treated as unrealistic. CISA reports and rule sets serve as regular test cases, and the presenters want to drop XML parsing because it introduces vulnerabilities.

The closing section shows the web interface, which offers interactive conversion, version diffing and shareable links. The roadmap includes plugging MISP modules into conversion for enrichment, adding CSV support, checking output against vendor profiles and building a public test corpus. Practitioners can use the hosted service or run the project on premises from its GitHub repository, with the aim of reducing friction between formats rather than achieving perfect mapping.

talks.title: NIST’s National Vulnerability Database Update and the Vulnerability Enrichment Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Explains how the National Vulnerability Database is reprioritizing CVE enrichment amid rising volume and a growing backlog.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how the National Vulnerability Database grew from a metadata layer on top of CVE identifiers into a source of product naming, weakness categorization and severity scores. It covers the addition of CPE product data, CWE classification and CVSS scoring, and how the expansion of CNAs from around 2016 let organizations publish CVE IDs directly. With roughly 502 CNAs now active, CVE volume has surged, and the speaker describes a backlog the NVD cannot keep up with, partly driven by more software hosted on GitHub.

To manage this, the NVD is moving to a risk-based model. CVEs on the KEV list are to be enriched within one business day, followed by software used across the federal government and critical software as defined under Executive Order 14028. Routine CVSS scoring of entries that already have a score will stop, with exceptions for scores that appear inconsistent with the evidence or when someone asks for a review. Older modified records are being set aside, and entries published before March 1 move to a "not scheduled" status. Work on LLM-based agents, deterministic automation and federated CPE management is underway.

The speaker stressed that data quality depends on its purpose, which is helping defenders decide what to patch first. Points raised include persistent reference links, consistent scoring and CNAs supplying more complete records at publication. The talk closed by asking the community for feedback, with a planned CPE workshop and a possible public GitHub channel for suggestions.

talks.title: Mind the Match: Why Vulnerability Matching Is Harder Than You Think
talks.teaser: Explains why vulnerability scanners disagree, how CPE and PURL matching fails, and how to verify and scale CVE triage.
talks.summary:
Lexi opens by challenging the assumption that running a vulnerability scanner yields a trustworthy CVE list. Scanner choice, SBOM generator behavior, and how lock files or manifests are produced all shape which dependencies appear and how they map to identifiers such as CPEs and PURLs before records in NVD, OSV, GHSA, or distro advisories are consulted. Normalization and fuzzy matching can surface real issues or flood teams with noise.

On a Red Hat 8 container image, Grype and Trivy reported 852 versus 3,719 findings—roughly 80.5% divergence. Case studies include kernel headers tied to kernel CVEs, Python setuptools missed at inventory time, and Tomcat JARs mapped through different Java indexes. Fix metadata, CVSS sources, and duplicate IDs across advisory namespaces add further disagreement. Experiments with mixed SBOM generators and scanners show large result drops when PURL qualifiers sit in fields only certain tools read, and SPDX versus CycloneDX can change Grype output even from the same image.

Practitioners should trace why a match fired, confirm packages and versions on the system, compare authoritative sources, and document suppressions so validation is not repeated. Pair generators with their intended scanners and upgrade them together. OSV helps collapse alias sprawl; pick a scoring hierarchy deliberately rather than stacking every scanner. Reuse prior verification work to cut manual triage at scale.

ZoomEye and anonymized Qualys telemetry show millions of internet and enterprise assets still on RSA-1024, TLS 1.0/1.1, RC4, and weak key exchange while post-quantum signals remain tiny. He reviews Shor versus Grover impacts, reuses legacy deprecation playbooks, scores priorities by weakness, impact, and migration effort, and warns PKI must migrate root-to-leaf without breaking monitoring. A vendor-neutral playbook covers discovery, VM-based ranking, owner engagement, governance, and crypto-agility purchasing rules.

talks.title: The CVE Program Quality Era: Strengthening Trust and Impact In Global Vulnerability Data
talks.teaser: Argues CVE quality spans record content, tooling, CNA participation and governance, and outlines the planned changes.
talks.summary:
Two representatives from CISA and MITRE present the CVE program's quality era as a system-wide problem, not a checklist for individual records. They trace the program's history from an early proof-of-value period through a scaling era in which many CNAs joined, and explain that growth has brought new strains on record completeness, validation and support for participants.

They walk through each layer of quality. Today a record technically needs only an identifier, a description, a public reference and ideally the affected product, so the presenters discuss requiring more data such as CVSS context and CWE root-cause mapping. They describe a reference archive to keep linked sources available, a data registry that lets CNAs manage their own details, and a new request and publication system in closed beta since March, with a planned May rollout. The new system offers real-time request status, self-service updates, verified domain ownership for vendors that are not CNAs, and phishing-resistant authentication. On governance, they stress transparent stewardship, a representative ecosystem, clearer decision-making and conflict-free participation, and propose expanding roots, including open-source groups, in a second federation phase. They also share figures on the shrinking share of CVEs assigned by MITRE or CISA.

The talk closes with a three-phase plan: establish a baseline, scale improvements across CNAs, then gather feedback. Audience questions covered whether the tooling could support closed coordination and how small volunteer open-source projects could take on CNA roles. The main takeaway is that record quality, participation and governance must evolve together, and the presenters favor public stewardship of the program.

talks.title: From JSON to Clarity: Practical Tools for SBOM Interpretation
talks.teaser: Presents a set of simple web tools that turn raw SBOM files into checks on quality, dependencies, licenses and age.
talks.summary:
SBOMs are now routine, yet many arrive as flat JSON files that are hard to interpret. Speakers from a corporate supply chain security team described frequent gaps: missing supplier data, absent dependency relationships, weak package identifiers and missing release dates. They presented five small browser-based tools, built with AI help, aimed at non-technical reviewers such as procurement and legal staff.

The first tool judges whether an SBOM is credible, flagging missing NTIA minimum elements, duplicate references and generic identifiers that block CVE mapping. The dependency analyzer separates direct from transitive components to show how a vulnerable or unlicensed library enters through a parent package. The CVE age tracker takes a pasted list and counts how long each issue has been public, using six months as an adjustable signal rather than a risk score. License analysis sorts components into risk categories and can attempt to retrieve unknown licenses, while version drift analysis compares the version in use with the latest release to flag dormant or archived projects.

The main takeaway is that exposing data already in an SBOM matters more than generating extra intelligence, since weak inputs weaken every later decision. The results can guide vendor questions and metadata requests, and accepted files feed continuous monitoring. Audience questions covered how end-of-life status is judged from repository archive state and how source-level analysis could complement these views.

talks.title: Contextual SBOMs: Unlocking Precise Vulnerability Management with Build-Time Content Intelligence
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Contextual SBOMs: Unlocking Precise Vulnerability Management with Build-Time Content Intelligence.
talks.summary: Red Hat’s Przemyslaw Roguski (“Rogue”) argues flat SPDX contains lists fail container responders because multi-stage Dockerfiles copy artifacts from builder images and base layers without provenance. Contextual SBOMs record descendant-of and build-tool-of relationships while monitoring each build step so analysts know whether a vulnerable curl binary arrived from a golang builder, a UBI base, or an application pip install. Examples contrast ambiguous http CVE tickets that ping-pong teams with precise routing: patch the base-image owner, rebuild downstream pipelines automatically, or notify application owners when compiled dependencies change. Complex demos map golang:latest intermediates, copied binaries, and numpy layers into a graph rather than a single flat inventory. Limitations include matching components without reliable PURLs, checksums, or package verification codes. Rogue points to the open Hermeto project for adoption and urges the SBOM ecosystem to strengthen identifiers so uncertain components can be flagged instead of guessed.

talks.title: CVE Record Format
talks.teaser: Explains how PURL and CPE applicability statements fit into the CVE record format and how to use them.
talks.summary:
The talk explains the CVE record format, the JSON schema that CNAs and authorized data publishers use to describe a CVE record. The speakers, both working group co-chairs on record quality, focus on two software identifiers added to it. The first is PURL, a URL-style identifier for packages that works across ecosystems. They walk through its parts, from type and namespace to name, qualifiers and subpath, and note that versions stay in the affected array for now.

The second is CPE, a structured naming scheme whose official dictionary NIST hosts, paired with CPE applicability statements that express logical conditions. Using NVD-style examples, they show version ranges, OR branches for separate lines of a product, and AND requirements such as an application running on specific hardware or OS. They explain that the older free-form CPE list was used inconsistently, since nothing said whether entries were fixed or broken versions. Both identifiers are optional, and CPE names should exist in NIST's dictionary before use.

In the question round, the speakers explain why neither identifier is mandatory: not every vendor or open-source project uses them, and the working groups still debate which fields should be required. Firmware remained an open question, since CPE forces a choice between hardware and OS. For practitioners, the main takeaway is that the record format now lets CNAs state which products and versions are affected in machine-readable form.

talks.title: Automating CNA CVE Reporting and Monthly Bulletins at Atlassian
talks.teaser: Shows how a CNA team automated CVE reservation, drafting and monthly bulletins using Jira Cloud workflows.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how a product security team moved its CVE program from a manual process of hand-written JSON records, spreadsheets and pull requests to an automated pipeline built on Atlassian Cloud. Before the change, only about 11% of first-party vulnerabilities were being disclosed, and data center customers, who patch on-premises instances on formal schedules, needed timely advisories to plan their maintenance.

The speakers walked through the building blocks: Jira automation rules, a Connect app that is being replaced by Forge, and CVE IDs reserved through the MITRE CVE Services API, sometimes in pooled blocks. A sanitization step turns patched bug bounty, pen test, internal review and software composition findings into draft public issues that a person reviews before release. Because version numbers are not linear, the team publishes explicit affected and fixed ranges for each release line. A monthly bulletin is then assembled from these drafts, with each engineering team checking its own items during a one-week review window, and products were aligned to a 28-day release cycle.

Reported outcomes include 240 CVEs disclosed over about three years, a 90% drop in CVE-related support questions, roughly 60 work weeks of engineering time saved, and customer upgrade time falling from about 91 days to 28 days. In the Q&A, the speakers said the support reduction came mostly from third-party findings, and that critical, actively exploited issues go through a separate crisis advisory process not covered in the talk. The practical takeaway is to automate CVE record creation first, test against the development API, and keep human review in the loop.

talks.title: Embracing the Era of Transparency: Automating VEX Application for Scalable, Context-Aware Security
talks.teaser: Covers NVIDIA's path from manual VEX on production-branch images to rule-based automation and Cosign-attached OpenVEX for OCI pulls.
talks.summary:
The session frames why large AI enterprise software stacks flood customers with scanner findings when container images bundle hundreds of dependencies and many CVEs. NVIDIA adopted vulnerability exploitability exchange records to state which issues are resolved, not affected, or still under review, starting with manually published records tied to pinned production-branch images on their container registry.

The speakers describe how demand outgrew manual work: an automated pipeline scans images, merges vendor VEX from Ubuntu and Red Hat, inherits rules from parent images, applies portfolio-wide policies, and routes ambiguous cases through agent-assisted analyst review before approval. They report roughly seven hundred thousand VEX documents published over two years, yet customers still escalate because VEX often stays at the catalog while images are retagged, mirrored, and scanned late in deployment without tool support.

The proposed direction attaches CycloneDX or OpenVEX data as OCI Cosign attestations so documents can travel with artifacts, with a live walkthrough using cosign commands and experimental Trivy VEX ingestion. Practitioners should treat publishing and consumption as separate problems: automate supplier-side assessments, then push ecosystem alignment so attestations survive registries and scanners honor them before go-live.

talks.title: The Vulnerability Ecosystem’s Vendor Bias
talks.teaser: Maps five vendor-biased failure modes in CVE handling for open source and argues for federated stewardship and richer context feeds.
talks.summary:
The speakers contrast a quarter-century of vulnerability coordination built around funded, centralized vendors with today’s open source reality: vast component sprains, often maintained by unpaid individuals, embedded in most commercial software. They describe an OSS CNA users group that surfaced recurring friction when upstream project CNAs are treated like enterprise manufacturers with full downstream visibility.

Peter Eller walks through five empirical biases: aggregators inflating severity beyond maintainer intent; equating vulnerable code with reachable risk despite data suggesting most bundled components are not reachable; misapplied environmental scoring and unclear authority among CNAs; volume and incentives crushing volunteer triage capacity; enterprise “fix it now” pressure versus responsible patch timelines; and disputed CVE labels that leave scanners showing unfixable findings and eroding trust. Yogish Mittal ties these to program-level responses rather than asking maintainers to become mini-vendors.

The closing argument favors a federated model: maintainers keep code truth while stewards and supplier programs such as EU-CERT-style roles and SSDP-style contextual feeds enrich records, including machine-readable dispute alternatives instead of binary vulnerable-or-not fights. Practitioners are urged to fix the coordination model, not blame the data—enterprises should demand context-aware risk decisions, aggregators should avoid worst-case defaults, and maintainers should use stewardship channels without owning every downstream support call.

talks.title: A Paradigm Shift in Vulnerability Identity: Why Vulnerability Databases Struggle
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of A Paradigm Shift in Vulnerability Identity: Why Vulnerability Databases Struggle.
talks.summary: Art Manion and Jay Jacobs argue vulnerability databases fail for philosophical, not engineering, reasons after two years trying to define a minimal viable CVE record. They tour Mill, Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Searle, and Kripke to show IDs must be meaningless pegs for evolving assertion clusters—not embedded descriptions like CPE strings that age poorly. Nine principles follow: shared vocabulary, global naming authorities, mutable records, bearer software identity, atomic survey-style fields, local language games, assertion provenance, machine-usable—not merely readable—data, and temporal distributed knowledge. They propose CVE governance moves toward assertion frameworks, richer X_ fields, and decentralized contributors without promising a single silver format.

talks.title: Axiomatic Events that Evolved Vulnerability Databases
talks.teaser: Traces the history of vulnerability databases from 1960s networking research through CVE and NVD.
talks.summary:
Johnny Shrive, a PhD student at the University of Tulsa, walks through how vulnerabilities came to be cataloged, starting with a 1967 report on computer security that predates the ARPANET. He covers the early network incidents that shaped the field, including a buffer overflow triggered by the first ARPANET message, the Creeper program and the Reaper response to it, and a structured list of Multics vulnerabilities from the early 1970s that already gave each issue a name, a type, a description and a remedy.

The middle of the talk moves through 1980s and 1990s events that pushed the community toward a shared catalog. These include the film WarGames, the tracking of an intruder described in The Cuckoo's Egg, the Morris worm, the Eligible Receiver 97 exercise, and the Solar Sunrise intrusions against military systems. Shrive then describes how work at MITRE, with input from CERT/CC and the wider community, led to CVE. He also traces the predecessors of the National Vulnerability Database, from an attack toolkit to ICAT, and the funding crises that nearly ended it before NVD was established in 2005.

He closes by arguing that relationships between a few willing people did much of the work behind these efforts. He also argues that asset ownership, more than scoring, drives most vulnerability backlogs, and that prioritizing by exploitation signals is more useful than chasing informational findings. For practitioners, the takeaway is that knowing how these catalogs were built helps explain the limits of the vulnerability data they use today.

talks.title: Fragile by Design: Large-Scale Evidence of Supply Chain Risk
talks.teaser: Shows how firmware and container images hide most components and CVEs from manifests, and why inventory comes before prioritization.
talks.summary:
The talk presents research from three years of analyzing firmware and container images, offered as data rather than a product pitch. The firmware data set covered almost 19,000 assets across more than 380 organizations, with 467 million vulnerability findings reducing to just under 500,000 unique vulnerabilities. Most components were invisible to manifests: almost 60% of firmware artifacts declared none, and about 99% of the vulnerabilities came from components the manifests did not show. In containers, 25% of components could only be identified through binary analysis.

A vendor with no CPEs in the National Vulnerability Database still had about 2.7 thousand CVEs on its devices, mostly from the Linux kernel, with the top ten components accounting for 93% of exposure. Old components with 1999-era CVEs, passwordless accounts, expired certificates and public and private keys on one device showed what goes unchecked. Filtering by network access, startup execution, EPSS, weaponization and the CISA KEV list narrowed the set to 414 with an EPSS score, 37 weaponized and 10 on KEV.

The second half covered trust and blast radius. Composition tools see downstream dependencies but not upstream ones, so a compromised package can enter overnight automated builds unnoticed. A study of Anthropic-related packages found 476 package names, 3,434 package versions and 127,000 direct or transitive package versions, with 202 million Docker Hub pulls. Contributor patterns such as working hours helped flag a malicious contributor to an open source pen testing project. The takeaways: build a complete inventory first, add trust context, and fail builds that break policy.

talks.title: The Myth of the Meteoric Rise in Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Traces how copied student PHP projects and loose CVE rules inflate vulnerability counts with duplicate entries.
talks.summary:
Scott Moore looks at why published vulnerability counts keep climbing, drawing on his years building the X-Force database that fed early CVE work. He walks through the chart's big jumps: a surge around 2005 after a public exploit database released large batches of entries, a 2014 case where a tool scanning Android apps led to 1,420 CVEs before MITRE asked the researchers to stop, and the 2015 wave of new CNAs that let organizations issue their own IDs.

The main argument is that since 2021, research CNAs have assigned IDs for reports they did not find themselves, and that many recent entries come from student PHP projects sold as downloadable source code. He downloaded 10 of these projects and found the same SQL injection in their login code, with one SourceCodester template hosted 369 times. Of the roughly 1,700 CVEs tied to these projects, he says only about 16% had been reported, and he estimates 15,243 more could be filed. In a separate test, he used an AI model on 15 WordPress plugins and reported 203 candidate issues; developers shipped fixes about two weeks later, with 175 still pending.

His takeaway is that real software such as WordPress should go through the normal disclosure process, while re-skinned repositories add noise that pollutes the vulnerability record. He admits he does not know who should enforce this, and the audience questions turned to how ecosystem advisories could be governed.

talks.title: AI Systems Are Software Systems
talks.teaser: Explains how existing vulnerability management, CVE rules and SBOM practices apply to AI software systems.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI systems are software systems and should fall under the same vulnerability management and secure-by-design practices as other software. The speaker, working within a federal scope, applies existing expectations: patch known exploited vulnerabilities, run a disclosure policy scoped to security issues, and decommission systems that no longer receive security updates. Buyers should write secure-by-design requirements into procurement, and existing guidance is mapped onto AI terms.

Much of the discussion covers familiar problems in new clothing. Naming, versioning and asset tracking are treated as existing challenges, and software bills of materials are cited through Deutsche Bahn, which processes 500,000 SBOMs a day with open-source tools. Models are described as a special kind of library. Applying CVE numbering authority rules, insecure default configurations and a Keras lambda layer case count as vulnerabilities, while most model misclassifications do not, unless they amount to a detection bypass or a trojanized model. Nondeterministic LLM output is compared to race conditions and is described as an engineering choice that could expose a seed.

The closing section separates system integrity, which usually drives a security response, from data and correctness integrity, which typically route to other teams. The speaker urges security teams to meet AI engineers early and to build checks into development pipelines, because faster code generation without them multiplies vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Diving into the CVSS Base Score Metrics - An Exploratory Analysis Bridging Product Security...
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Diving into the CVSS Base Score Metrics - An Exploratory Analysis Bridging Product Security....
talks.summary: Panasonic Project Astrea researchers Kohe Taguchi and Yuji Kikuchi challenge medium-severity CVSS complacency on IoT appliances using 424 medium base-score CVEs from 2023–2024 plus honeypot telemetry. Examples include MFP HTTP PUT validation bypass and misconfigured admin APIs that chain into takeover despite modest scores. They cluster frequent attack-vector and impact metric combinations—network reachability with improper access control dominates OT and router classes—and correlate honeypot exploitation of CVE-2020-14181 style user-enumeration probes. Yuichi maps CWE frequency in internal security testing—information exposure and vulnerable dependencies rank high—against honeypot-leading injection, path traversal, and missing-authentication flaws, arguing developers see design-layer weaknesses while attackers chase unauthenticated execution endpoints. The speakers call for lifecycle-linked analysis connecting root-cause testing data, shipment incidents, and public CVE trends rather than single-axis CVSS triage, acknowledging sample bias and the need to align private scoring with NVD metrics.

talks.title: Accuracy Is Not Enough: Detecting Hidden Risk in CVE Impact Prediction
talks.teaser: Shows how accuracy hides costly false negatives in CVE impact assessment, and proposes trust metrics like MCC to track them over time.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at deciding whether a newly published CVE affects a given environment. Configuration, enabled plugins, sandboxing and network exposure change the answer, and vendors such as Red Hat, SUSE, Debian and NIST often rate the same bug differently. Headline accuracy can hide the errors that matter most: in a hypothetical set of ten CVEs, one case only wastes effort on a false positive, while the other misses a 9.8 OpenSSL flaw entirely, yet both score 90% accuracy.

False negatives leave customers exposed, while false positives mainly cost engineering effort and reboot downtime, so the speaker treats false negatives as the higher risk in vulnerability management. A disputed record, CVE-2023-48022, shows how verdicts shift: the CNA first said not affected, an ADP source later said affected, and the status became disputed. Automating on that status turns the earlier miss into a catch. The speaker proposes tracking false negative rate, negative likelihood ratio and the Matthews correlation coefficient over rolling windows, such as weekly, per package or group, so a trust score moves up or down as new evidence arrives.

The metrics can be computed from fields already in CVE-style records, such as default status and ADP-related fields. The speaker argues the same approach suits any classifier that must show correctness to customers. The takeaway is to watch sources that revise verdicts and chart error types over time instead of relying on one accuracy figure. An open-source version of the dashboard was announced as forthcoming.

talks.title: Organizational Context Matters: Security Control Effectiveness on Vulnerabilities for Prioritization
talks.teaser: Explains re-scoring vulnerabilities with simulated attack results and existing security control effectiveness to reprioritize patching.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that base CVSS scores alone overwhelm teams working through growing vulnerability lists, and that prioritization should also reflect whether an organization's existing controls actually stop the attacker behavior behind each flaw. The speakers describe a customer whose scanners reported about 29,000 vulnerabilities, with millions of vulnerable instances across assets, and where 68% of findings were high or critical on base scores.

The approach maps each CVE to a library of about 30,000 simulated attack actions, then checks through simulation how often those behaviors are blocked. Manual mapping was slow, sometimes taking an hour or more per CVE and depending on the analyst, so an AI agent now matches CVEs to actions in about a minute and attaches a confidence score. Two examples were shown. An n8n remote code execution flaw dropped from a base score of 10 to 8 after the attack vector, attack complexity and privileges were adjusted for the controls in place. An Active Directory flaw involving delegated and group managed service accounts, mapped to an action blocked 99% of the time on average, moved from 8.8 to 8.1.

The final step combines base CVSS, contextual CVSS, business criticality, exploitability and control effectiveness into an exposure score. That score can raise some medium or high findings to critical when many related actions go unblocked. The takeaway is that CVSS alone is not enough: map vulnerabilities to attack actions, measure control effectiveness, and then reprioritize the operational list.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The AI Arms Race in Vulnerability Management, Who’s Winning?.
talks.summary: Pluto security researcher Yotam frames vulnerability management under collapsing time-to-exploit curves—median disclosure-to-exploitation windows shrinking toward hours per Zero Day Clock visualizations—while attackers weaponize the same LLM capabilities defenders experiment with. He walks milestone events from Log4Shell through 2024 agentic one-day exploitation papers, Google Big Sleep’s AI-found SQLite bug, Anthropic’s hundreds of upstream fixes, and Mythes claims of hundred-fold exploit-writing gains on decades-old BSD flaws. Offense benefits from fewer organizational constraints than patch orchestration, and AI-assisted coding expands attack surface with weak secure-by-default incentives. Yotam urges defenders to invest in reachability and business context engineering for models, prioritize remediation automation over discovery arms races, govern MCP and skill supply chains, focus on root-cause hardening instead of CVE whack-a-mole, and explore deception tuned to agentic attackers. He closes noting attackers may already outpace defenders unless assumptions are reset.

talks.title: AI Is Writing Your Bug Reports. Can You Tell?
talks.teaser: Shows how to triage polished vulnerability reports by weighing evidence over fluent writing, using three case studies.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a gap facing vulnerability disclosure programs: report intake has grown in volume and polish, while triage has not kept pace. The speaker argues that a well-written report is not necessarily well substantiated, and that the bigger risk is a fast but wrong triage decision. She points to curl ending its public bug bounty in early 2026, and to a reported 224% rise in report volume over a 90-day window, with low-quality AI-generated submissions described as a major operational problem.

The session is built around three reports that the audience voted on as human-written, AI-written, or a mix. The first described a critical unauthenticated remote code execution with a high CVSS score, yet contradicted itself on whether authentication was needed, and its CVE identifier turned out to be hallucinated. The second, a privilege escalation through support bundle upload, was judged human-found but AI-packaged: the core bug was plausible, while the claimed full environment takeover was never backed by evidence. The third, an authentication bypass in a report download endpoint, was plain and brief, with exact replay steps and observed behaviour, and most of the room correctly read it as human-written.

The takeaways are practical. At intake, ask for product version, environment, authentication state and expected versus actual behaviour. In follow-up, ask one or two domain-specific questions that a padded report cannot answer. Separate the confirmed bug from the claimed blast radius and score only what has been verified. The speaker closes with a mnemonic built around pausing before scoring: parse the claim, ask for artifacts, understand preconditions, score confirmed impact, and evolve the workflow.

talks.title: Remediation-Aware Reachability: Patching Containers, Prioritizing with Agentic-CTI, and Scaling...
talks.teaser: Argues that vulnerability triage needs ownership, reachability and threat intelligence, and introduces an open platform for it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by arguing that disclosed vulnerabilities, now above 300,000 and growing about 25% a year, have outpaced defenders, and that AI hype makes the situation harder. The speaker says a workable program needs asset ownership, the place each flaw lives, and evidence that something can actually reach it. Attacks on package ecosystems, such as the Axios incident, and exploitation windows shrinking from weeks to under a day show why scanner-driven triage falls behind.

The middle section proposes sorting findings by evidence rather than CVSS score alone. Paper tigers are high-severity issues with no sign of exploitation, while tier one items show exploitation, ransomware use or fast acceleration. Inputs include prediction scores, bug bounty activity, forked proof-of-concept code and a re-indexed NVD of 343,000 entries mapped to CWE, CAPEC and TTP. For npm, a 77-parameter model screens packages before LLM analysis, a judge model and human approval, and the speaker says the path from initial malware exploitation to publication takes 15 minutes.

The talk closes by introducing Phoenix Blue, an open-source threat intelligence platform that processes about 2 million advisories every hour, with access through an MCP server or API for agents. Companion parts cover reachability and remediation. The main takeaway is that AI should serve as a tool fed with high-quality data, while humans keep the final decision.

talks.title: Production Is the New Attack Surface: Why Post-Deployment Endpoint Detection Is Now Critical
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders must watch running production, using SBOMs and deployment data to match new CVEs to live endpoints.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that most security effort goes into finding and fixing flaws before software ships, leaving the running production environment under-defended. Opening with the disruption of satellite communications during the Ukrainian war, the talk stresses that hard-to-patch systems such as satellites, fighter jets and edge devices are exposed. Figures presented as averages include a 200% rise in vulnerabilities over three years, about 47 critical and high-risk findings per day, and a repair cost of roughly 10,000 to 50,000 dollars per vulnerability.

The proposed remedy is a digital twin of production. For each release, the speaker keeps the SBOM, the Git repository and endpoint details such as a Helm chart or Kubernetes audit logs. That record is synced continuously against vulnerability data such as OSV, so newly published CVEs can be matched to packages already running, rather than waiting for periodic rescans. An AI step could then open an issue for risky upgrades or a pull request for simple ones, with the goal of addressing runtime supply chain issues within one day. Agent-based tools were described as heavy, slow to deploy and hard to run on constrained environments, and containers make inventory harder.

In the questions, the audience noted that the approach depends on SBOM accuracy. The speaker agreed that better SBOMs, removing unreachable packages and adding attestation and provenance data would strengthen it. The talk closes by inviting contributors to the Ortelius project, which is incubating at the Continuous Delivery Foundation, along with its CI/CD security guide.

talks.title: Vulnerabilities Without CVEs: Governing the Dark Matter of Internal and Unknown Software
talks.teaser: Shows how host telemetry from process, network and file activity can reveal risky software that scanners never flag.
talks.summary:
Vulnerability management programs mostly see software that can be matched to a product name, a version and a public CVE. Much of what attackers use falls outside that model: abandoned vendor appliances, internal tools written by someone who has since left, forgotten migration services and utilities baked into gold images. These run with real privileges and network reach, yet produce no finding, so the risk never reaches the queue that leadership tracks.

The talk argues that instead of guessing from outside with banners, ports and file hashes, defenders should ask the host itself what happened. Process lineage, listeners, outbound connections, file access and configuration changes can be correlated by process ID to build a defensible finding even when no CVE exists. The speaker walks through the OS primitives for this: Microsoft Detours for application-level call logging, ETW on Windows, eBPF with LSM hooks on Linux, and the Endpoint Security Framework plus a network extension on macOS. Case studies include a legacy PDF converter with command injection and outbound egress, an unknown service reading a customer database and writing bulk data to S3, and a binary that fetched URLs pointing at the cloud metadata address. Other patterns covered include disabled TLS certificate validation, unquoted service paths and cross-process memory access.

The practical takeaway is to create "synthetic CVE" findings from host evidence and route them through the existing queue, severity scale, SLAs and dashboards. Since these issues often cannot be patched, remediation means hardening, blocking, monitoring, isolating or decommissioning. The speaker suggests starting with three patterns and a small set of telemetry sources.
