talks.title: Episode 56: Mor Weinberger and Lior Kaplan, FIRSTCON26 Speakers
talks.teaser: Traces 10,000 open source CVEs from disclosure to applied fix, and why patches often sit unapplied for months.
talks.summary:
This episode of the FIRST Impressions podcast features Mor Weinberger and Lior Kaplan, ahead of their FIRST conference talk on what happens between a CVE being published and a fix reaching end users. Weinberger describes past work in runtime and supply chain security, and current work building container images free of known CVEs by compiling popular open source projects such as Postgres and Redis from source. The pair scanned the most popular open source projects daily for a year, tracking more than 40 CVE journeys from publication through detection, fix, and a clean image.

Their data showed that about 90% of CVEs already had a fix available but not applied, and around 40% stayed in container images for more than six months. They split the journey into discovery, fix creation, delivery through the supply chain, and adoption by users. Gaps include slow review of submissions, fixes that take time to propagate through dependencies, and users who wait for maintenance windows. Upgrades can also break APIs or introduce new bugs. In their analysis, minimal images removed roughly 40 to 50 percent of CVEs, and higher-severity issues were more likely to receive fixes.

For practitioners, the speakers suggest starting with the remediation steps that have the most impact, planning around the areas that are hardest to upgrade, and remembering that many fix authors are volunteers. They also argued that companies should identify a handful of core open source projects to fund, since visibility into their own dependencies is often poor.

talks.title: Episode 55: Merike Kaeo, FIRSTCON26 Program Chair
talks.teaser: Previews the FIRST conference program's balance of incident response topics, automation, and outreach to smaller organizations.
talks.summary:
This episode of the First Impressions podcast interviews Merike Kaeo, program chair for FIRSTCON26, the FIRST conference being held in Denver, Colorado, from June 14 to 19, 2026. She explains that the year's theme, peak defense and building adaptive systems for modern threats, takes its inspiration from the mountains near Denver and reflects the need to stay flexible, resilient and willing to learn as threats and automation tools change quickly.

She describes how a 27-member program committee built a deliberately balanced program and kept the number of AI and large language model talks limited to avoid hype. The topics range from threat intelligence tooling, enhanced incident response and vulnerability disclosure to victim notification, tabletop exercises, SOC and CSIRT maturity, information sharing, nation-state activity, product security and software development lifecycle tools, and standards. Sessions are pitched from basic to advanced levels, and two keynotes are planned, one from a former SolarWinds executive and one from a former NSA deputy director.

Kaeo says her own interest lies in operational efficiency and automation, especially how AI-enabled tools can help teams detect, mitigate and resolve incidents faster once they occur. She also raised the gap facing small and medium businesses, many of which lack operational incident response plans and cannot afford outsourced SOC teams, and mentioned a project she led to create response plans for schools. She closes by encouraging listeners to explore first.org and attend the regional FIRST events held through the year, such as a recent one in Munich.

talks.title: Improving Security Across Nations with FIRST: Carlos Leonardo, FIRST Board of Directors Member
talks.teaser: Explains how FIRST membership and a national CSIRT help countries build incident response capacity and regional cooperation.
talks.summary:
This short talk makes the case for joining FIRST from the viewpoint of a national incident response leader. It traces how the Dominican Republic's national CSIRT became, in December 2020, the first such team in the Caribbean to join FIRST. The speaker says several other public and private organisations in the country have joined since then, bringing the count to four FIRST members, with more expected.

The middle of the talk covers how the national CSIRT was built alongside the national cybersecurity strategy and a national cybersecurity center, drawing on FIRST guidance and practices from the OAS and countries such as Spain and Estonia. Trust was built with military, financial, energy and telecommunications sectors, and the national team now runs two-way information sharing so it can support sector teams' detection and response. The speaker also describes passing lessons to other regional countries, and cyber diplomacy work in UN working groups on responsible ICT use and the cybercrime convention, arguing that incidents now reach political decision-makers and international law.

The closing section notes that Latin American countries still face knowledge gaps and limited budgets, and that FIRST helps through capacity-building programmes, open-source frameworks and tools. The speaker encourages practitioners, whether starting out or leading established teams, to take part in FIRST events, discussions and trainings.

talks.title: Episode 51: Cornelia Puhze, FIRSTCON25 Speaker
talks.teaser: Makes the case that awareness training should explain how social engineering manipulates emotions, not only list warning signs.
talks.summary:
This First Impressions podcast interview, recorded ahead of the FIRST conference in Copenhagen, features Cornelia Puhze, co-chair of the FIRST special interest group on human factors in security. She previews her talk on helping people resist social engineering as generative tools make manipulation cheaper. Her central argument is that awareness programmes have focused on rule-based clues such as writing style or images, and seldom explain how attackers exploit emotions like urgency, fear and excitement.

She draws on the idea of fast, automatic thinking versus slow, deliberate thinking, noting that attackers push targets into the fast mode so they cannot pause and reason. Suggested defences include teaching the adversarial mindset, recognising workplace pressures such as tight deadlines and deference to authority, and building a pause habit. As an example she describes a breathing-based stop method, breaking off a call, and checking with a colleague or another channel. The interview also covers a relative who sensed a cryptocurrency scam but still transferred money, leading her to suggest a strict rule: end contact whenever a gut feeling arises.

The discussion closes on how people who click phishing links are often tired or distracted rather than uninformed, so shaming them is counterproductive and inbox habits matter. Organisations would need a culture change, since experienced staff may no longer notice when they pause. A written article on the research, first published in German and later in English, is available on the speaker's organisation website.

talks.title: Hard Problems in CWE, and What it Tells us about Hard Problems in the Industry
talks.teaser: Explains why mapping weaknesses to CWE entries is hard and how the CWE project is trying to improve its taxonomy.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the open problems facing the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) project, now nearly twenty years old. The speaker traces how its audience has shifted from code analysis tool vendors and researchers toward vulnerability management staff who publish CVE records every day. The taxonomy grew from an early collection of inputs into a layered structure of pillars, classes, bases and variants, and newer domains such as hardware, ICS and AI are being added through public community contributions.

The middle section focuses on mapping accuracy. The speaker explains why the same vulnerability can be classified differently: terms like buffer overflow, stack overflow and memory leak mean different things to different people, root cause analysis demands language and domain knowledge, and one weakness often sits downstream of another. Examples include choosing the broad CWE-77 when the narrower CWE-78 fits, and defaulting to CWE-20 for input validation when better children exist. Mapping usage notes that mark entries as allowed, discouraged or prohibited are presented as a way to steer users toward specific entries. Classification gaps, such as access control, and cross-cutting proposals that do not fit a single hierarchy are also covered.

The closing section outlines planned work: clearer intermediate entries, better recognition for newer technologies, retiring outdated entries with minimal disruption, and formalizing dimensions for a future major version. The speaker also answered audience questions about AI-assisted recategorization, forward compatibility and trend analysis. The takeaway for practitioners is to map to the most specific weakness available, and to treat a high-level mapping as a sign of a gap in the taxonomy rather than a simple error.

talks.title: When it Comes to Managing Risk, Context is King
talks.teaser: Argues that context beats raw CVSS scores when prioritizing an ever-growing flood of vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works on vulnerability scanning content, argues that teams stuck on high and critical CVSS scores are racing a backlog that never ends, since published CVEs reached roughly 40,000 in 2024. CVSS was built to describe worst-case severity, not likelihood, so memory bugs that might only crash a system often score as remote code execution. Temporal and environmental metrics can lower scores, but he warns that tuning them too aggressively can hide lateral movement risk from machines that seem unimportant.

Next he focuses on exploitation signals. Only about 13% of 2024 CVEs had public proof-of-concept code, and under 1% had known active exploitation. CISA's known-exploited list, around 1,300 entries, gives a short, defensible set to fix and a measurable way to show risk going down. He treats EPSS as a useful but black-box probability of exploitation within 28 days, noting that many high-scoring CVEs were never exploited while half of the known-exploited ones sit below 0.1.

For emerging headlines, he weighs scope, ease of exploitation and attack, ease of remediation, proof-of-concept availability and in-the-wild activity. A printing-service flaw looked alarming but needed chaining and a non-default setup, while a zero-day in an internet-facing VPN with an authentication bypass warranted fast action. He closes by urging defensible SLAs, planned responses to known patch cycles, automation for low-risk software, and urgent deadlines reserved for confirmed threats so that trust in alerts holds.

talks.title: Managing Risk Across the Vulnerability Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Shows how one company ties supplier vetting, SBOM inventories and vulnerability response into one product security program.
talks.summary:
The panel presents a product security program built around knowing exactly which third-party and open-source components go into each release. Product teams register their component inventories during the build, and those inventories are checked for format and required fields before they enter a dependency management platform. Outbound SBOMs are produced in SPDX 2.3. An open-source trustworthiness score and a trusted repository are being introduced to steer developers toward better component choices earlier, though the score is currently guidance rather than a hard gate.

On the supplier side, onboarding starts with an inherent risk assessment, followed by a security questionnaire, a risk rating, and then corrective action plans, contract terms, or an accepted risk. Continuous monitoring follows. After onboarding, unresolved fixes move through a two-level escalation, from the product team to the supplier and then to the response team, and can end in a conversation between vice presidents. Metrics such as how long a supplier takes to deliver a fix feed back into supplier trust scores.

The product security response team plans to use these inputs to open tickets automatically for affected product teams when a dependency issue appears, and to track supplier advisories and VEX statements against supplier SBOMs. Advisories and VEX data are to be published through an API so customers can see whether they are affected. The presenters argued that an SBOM is a static record of a release while VEX is dynamic, so the two should be kept separate. Binary-based comparison is a longer-term goal, while source-based inventories are used today. The takeaway is that a complete, well-formatted inventory underpins everything else.

talks.title: Context Matters: Qualitative Insights into Developers’ Approaches and Challenges with Software...
talks.teaser: Reports interviews with 20 developers on where software composition analysis tools lack the context needed to act on alerts.
talks.summary:
Elizabeth, a PhD student in the Whisper Lab at NC State, presents a user study of software composition analysis (SCA) tools, which flag known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries. She opens with the Log4j incident to show why teams rely on these scanners, then walks through a scan of a public repository. One transitive library produced a long list of alerts and several possible upgrade paths, which made it unclear what to do.

The research drew on semi-structured interviews of about 45 minutes each with 20 industry professionals who use SCA tools. The main finding was that context is missing at several points. Alerts carry generic vulnerability information, so teams spend extra effort judging whether they are actually affected. Automatic scans in CI can halt pipelines when they are noisy, and some teams moved to running scans by hand. Sharing results across teams and suppliers adds overhead. Participants also described unsupported languages, uneven support across package ecosystems, binary scanning that struggles with copied or modified code, and fixes that break APIs after major-version upgrades.

Practitioners described prioritising by severity, reachability and network exposure, and some accepted risk or isolated components when updates were too costly. The talk closes with suggestions for tools: add function reachability, infrastructure and network context, exploitability based on data flow, combining SCA with SAST, and feedback loops from users. The practical takeaway is to pick a tool that fits your pipeline and to make sure the context needed to judge impact is available.

talks.title: Exploited CVEs of 2024: Lessons for Vendors and Defenders
talks.teaser: Maps 2024 vulnerabilities with public exploitation evidence and shows where scoring systems fall short for defenders.
talks.summary:
Patrick Garrity, a researcher at VulnCheck, looks at vulnerabilities whose exploitation was first publicly reported in 2024. He counts around 800 so far, backed by over 2,000 reference citations from more than 100 sources, and notes the number keeps growing as late evidence surfaces. He explains how exploitation evidence is defined, pointing to sources beyond CISA's KEV catalog such as Project Zero, Shadow Server and Microsoft's advisories. He reports 53 of these vulnerabilities with a known ransomware association. He also flags bias in the data, including a Shadow Server onboarding that pulled in 2023 disclosures and roughly 62 WordPress plugin issues added through coordination with CNAs.

He groups affected products by target area, such as network edge devices, operating systems, content management systems, virtualization, backups and email, so teams can assign patch processes and controls. On scoring, the severity spread of exploited vulnerabilities looks much like the overall CVSS distribution, and CVSS-BT changes it only marginally, mainly at the top scores. Many exploited 2024 vulnerabilities had low EPSS scores, and the newer V4 model scored them higher after retraining, though its long-term accuracy is still unproven.

His takeaways are to act on public exploitation evidence and weaponization with urgency regardless of score, to understand the limits of scoring systems, and to tackle vulnerability debt through root cause analysis, end-of-life pruning and mitigating controls. In the Q&A he warned that relying on scores alone is very risky.

talks.title: Building a PSIRT for a Standards Organization
talks.teaser: Shows how a standards body built a product security response team, and the governance and disclosure lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes how a standards organization, the Trusted Computing Group, set up a product security incident response capability after members worried that flaws were being handled unevenly and disclosed inconsistently. A vulnerability response subcommittee met for ten months, collected more than 150 substantive comments, and produced a guidelines-style framework. That framework recommends a separate response team whose members are nominated by the board, approved by the oversight subcommittee, and kept in place even when board membership changes.

The talk distinguishes resolving a report from resolving a vulnerability, since most incoming items must be passed to the member or working group that owns the fix. It covers a team of four to six responders, round-robin assignment of incidents, and separate handling for vendor product flaws, specification defects, reference code problems, and reports outside the group's scope. Multi-party issues go to outside coordinators, and the speaker warns that overlapping internal and external reporting can cause confusion. Confidentiality expectations differed from those of a standards group, and some board members feared losing control of intellectual property, which took considerable reassurance to resolve. Publication approvals were streamlined so that any two officers can sign off, and legal hours were pre-allocated for emergencies.

The team was stood up in 2019 and expects one to three incidents a year. The speaker's takeaways include making constrained one-on-one requests to subject matter experts, defining publishing and decision processes in advance, reviewing membership requirements, checking older code for historical flaws, and keeping oversight separate from operations.

talks.title: Operationalizing SSVC
talks.teaser: Walks through CISA's SSVC decision tree, showing how repeatable scoring turns vulnerability triage into stakeholder action.
talks.summary:
CISA's vulnerability management team uses the Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) model to triage disclosures. The presenters argue that CVSS describes technical severity well but ignores each stakeholder's environment, and that tens of thousands of yearly disclosures need a repeatable method. SSVC, built with the Software Engineering Institute, is a decision tree that starts with exploitation state, then weighs automatability and technical impact, with mission prevalence and well-being added internally. Paths end in track, monitor, attend, or act.

CISA has used SSVC since April 2020 and began publishing the first three decision points for new CVEs through its enrichment work and authorized data publisher role. Since full enrichment began around February 2024, roughly 46,000 vulnerabilities have been scored, with under 10 percent carried to a final outcome, about 8 percent actioned, 3 percent landing on act and about 5 percent on attend. One example was CVE-2023-20593, an AMD chip flaw that scored 9.8 under CVSS. Because the conditions needed for exploitation were missing from almost all affected devices, the team scored it track.

Acting on outcomes falls to a partner team that mostly communicates through alerts, advisories and targeted notices, with emergency directives at the far end. The presenters stressed buy-in from analysts, executives and incident responders, and said that friction means the tree should be revised. Separate trees for federal and operational technology settings are being explored, and the guide and calculator are on CISA's SSVC page.

talks.title: Securing Citizen Developers: A New Opportunity to Build Safe Applications
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Securing Citizen Developers: A New Opportunity to Build Safe Applications.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at VulnCon, Kayla Underoffer, Lead Security Engineer in the CTO office at Zenity, explores the rapid rise of citizen developers and the new security challenges and opportunities they bring. Underoffer begins by examining historical lessons learned from "shift left" initiatives in traditional software engineering—where mismatched expectations, alert fatigue, and security acting as a delivery blocker hindered progress. She argues that low-code/no-code platforms and AI agents represent a "new hope" to establish security practices effectively from the outset, provided security teams learn to collaborate with business makers, leverage native platform capabilities, and apply automated guardrails.

### Key Topics
- **Lessons from Traditional Shift Left:** Shift-left approaches often struggled due to misaligned expectations between engineering and security, overwhelming volumes of vulnerabilities and false positives, and small security teams acting as bottlenecks.
- **The Rise of Citizen Developers:** Business users in domains such as finance, HR, and marketing are building applications, complex workflows, and autonomous AI agents using enterprise low-code/no-code platforms. According to Zenity's 2024 report, organizations averaged over 79,000 such applications, with an average 39.1% year-over-year growth rate.
- **The Citizen Development Lifecycle:** Unlike standard engineering processes, the citizen development lifecycle is typically owned entirely by the business, focusing purely on rapid creation without formal software development life cycles, iteration, or security/IT involvement.
- **Build-Time vs. Runtime Risks:** Risks are split between build-time design choices (e.g., misconfigured connections) and runtime agent actions (e.g., autonomous triggers, prompt injection, and data exfiltration).

### Technical Details
Underoffer details how configuration choices at build time directly dictate an application's or agent's attack surface in runtime:
- **Top Build-Time Risks:** Zenity's 2024 report highlights authorization misuse, authentication failures, and improper data/secrets handling as the primary risks.
- **Authorization Misuse:** Illustrated via a credit approval agent where an action connector was configured to use the creator's personal credentials (Chris interacting with Salesforce). When shared across an organization, all users effectively act under Chris's permissions.
- **Authentication Failures:** Illustrated with an agent ("hackerbot v2") connected to internal SharePoint data that was left completely unauthenticated, making internal critical data publicly accessible.
- **Secrets Handling:** Citizen developers frequently hard-code plaintext credentials and API keys into workflows due to a lack of security background.
- **Runtime & AI Agent Risks:** Illustrated through an autonomous email support agent triggered by incoming messages where the maker failed to filter the "From" address field, exposing the agent to runtime manipulation, sensitive data exfiltration, or indirect prompt injection.

### Takeaways & Remediation Strategy
Underoffer outlines a four-part framework tailored to low-code/no-code ecosystems:
1. **Visibility & Inventory:** Overcome "shadow environments" by leveraging enterprise platform features and third-party tools to inventory who is building what, prioritizing environments holding critical business data.
2. **Risk Assessment:** Evaluate the "how" of application design and rely heavily on automated scanning, as manual penetration testing is still underdeveloped in these ecosystems.
3. **Remediation:** Take advantage of platform controls for "silent remediation"—such as programmatically stripping sensitive data from logs or changing authentication and guest access settings automatically at the environmental level, supplemented by automated outreach for manual fixes.
4. **Prevention & Culture:** Enforce environmental-level guardrails to remove insecure options from makers, meet business users where they work (rather than expecting them in Jira/ServiceNow), and pair automated fixes with clear educational feedback. Underoffer highlights a referenced BlueHat talk featuring Microsoft and Zenity, where an under-five-person team reduced organizational low-code/no-code risk by 90% in four months.

talks.title: Identifying and Assigning AI Model Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Examines whether AI flaws fit today's CVE, CVSS and disclosure processes, and which new frameworks could handle them.
talks.summary:
The talk, from two RAND Corporation researchers, starts with the current vulnerability ecosystem: CVE identifiers, CWE weakness types, CVSS severity scores and coordinated disclosure. It then asks whether AI flaws fit that system. The speakers split them into three groups: conventional bugs in AI frameworks, which fit existing CVE handling; model behavior flaws such as prompt injection, which have no code error to patch; and ethics and safety failures such as biased hiring tools.

A side-by-side comparison showed gaps on the AI side. There is no central catalog like the NVD, and AI bug bounty platforms are less mature than traditional ones. Two emerging proposals were presented. The coordinated flaw disclosure framework adds structured reporting, extended model cards and an independent adjudication panel, and was piloted at DEF CON 32. The coordinated disclosure of dual-use capabilities proposal works as an early warning system that sends risky findings to a central clearing house.

The second half covered a RAND project on how AI could change vulnerability volume. Examples included AI-assisted code analysis and fuzzing, which could help defenders but also help attackers find weak points, and lower skill barriers for exploitation. The researchers said their open questions include which actors would benefit most, and they plan interviews and policy work. The takeaway: model behavior flaws need a new framework, while software bugs can stay in the existing process.

Panelists describe how their organizations weigh customer impact, disclosure, and whether a vulnerability can be tied to a recognizable product. They also consider how CVE records help researchers and security teams share information, alongside direct customer notices and other ways providers communicate fixes.

talks.title: Managing Vulnerabilities through SSDLC
talks.teaser: Covers a product security lifecycle from threat modeling to vulnerability response, with pain points and lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how a team that delivers open source projects applies a secure software development lifecycle, and what it has learned while putting that process into practice. Rather than a one-off task, the process runs as a loop: threat modeling comes first, followed by static code analysis, vulnerability scanning, penetration testing and vulnerability response, with security documentation sitting on top of all of it.

Product teams carry out threat modeling themselves, with central guidance. They set the scope, identify crown jewels and stepping stones, map data flows and trust boundaries, then record threats, existing and planned controls, and residual risk. Common pitfalls include leaving out built-in controls such as TLS, which can fail, and letting scope grow until the exercise can never be finished. Static analysis runs in CI so it becomes routine, but no tool covers everything, and a clean result can create false confidence. Scanners only flag known vulnerabilities, give different results from one another, and need repeated runs on each artifact for as long as it is supported.

On the response side, the talk argues that vulnerabilities should be handled as business as usual rather than as a panic. That means defined support lifetimes, prioritising by severity, offering mitigations early and communicating clearly with users. Threat models also help focus third-party pentests. Security documentation should be written for different personas and cover risks, sensitive functions, cryptography, how-to guides and hardening guides. The takeaway is that you can mitigate, avoid, transfer or accept a risk, but ignoring it is not an option.

talks.title: Merging Security and Compliance: Perspectives on Emerging Regulations and Best Practices
talks.teaser: Breaks down how the EU Cyber Resilience Act shapes open source responsibilities and how a shared security baseline helps.
talks.summary:
The panel introduces the EU Cyber Resilience Act and explains why it reaches far beyond Europe: any organisation selling products with digital elements into the EU is affected. A Linux Foundation study of 600 upstream contributors found that most were unfamiliar with the law. The speakers sort affected parties into three groups: manufacturers, who face fines; open source stewards, with lighter obligations; and maintainers who do not sell into the EU and carry no legal liability for their projects.

Vulnerability handling is a central concern. Manufacturers must give notice of actively exploited or severe vulnerabilities within 24 hours, publish an advisory within 72 hours and finish a report about a month later. Reporting requirements start in December 2026, with full effect at the end of 2027. The speakers urge companies to fund and contribute to the upstream projects they rely on, since forking a fast-moving project such as Kubernetes quickly becomes costly and risky.

To bridge compliance and engineering, the speakers present the Open Source Project Security Baseline, a set of 41 requirements in three maturity levels, with level one aimed at single-maintainer projects. They estimate that following it gives evidence for 19 of the 21 CRA Annex I requirements, leaving out handling of personal data. Their practical advice is to engage upstream and to keep verifiable evidence of practices such as signed attestations.

talks.title: Ask Not Whether CVSSv3.1 and v4 Scores are Inconsistent, But What Can You Do About It
talks.teaser: Explains why CVSS v3.1 and v4.0 scores disagree and proposes consistency rules to align ratings across both versions.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why CVSS v3.1 and v4.0 scores often disagree for the same vulnerability, and what analysts can do about it. The speakers recall earlier reports of scoring variation across vendors. They attribute much of it to human judgement, subjective readings of short descriptions, and copying errors, such as a description apparently reused for a neighbouring CVE ID.

The study maps how metrics changed between versions. Prompting a large language model with metric names, the team found it scored lowest for attack vector, privileges required and impact. They defined rules: one-to-one mappings for metrics like attack vector, one-to-many for user interaction and attack complexity, and a many-to-many treatment of scope, which v4 splits into vulnerable and subsequent system impact. On a public set of over 2,000 CVEs, user interaction conflicted in 22.1% of entries while other metrics mostly agreed. A private set of over 6,000 CVEs showed 26.7% impact conflicts at one company, and 3.3% still conflicted after that company applied its internal agreement rules.

The practical advice is to rate both versions together, or to derive one from the other using the rules, so mismatches surface early. They stressed that v4 is still in early adoption and asked for more v4 data. They closed with open questions: which version to trust for patching when both exist, and whether the v4 severity formula could bring the two closer together.

talks.title: Towards a Vulnerability Reporting Specification
talks.teaser: Presents a draft vulnerability management specification for open source projects, aimed at EU Cyber Resilience Act requirements.
talks.summary:
The Eclipse Foundation's Open Regulatory Compliance working group is drafting a vulnerability management specification to help open source projects and manufacturers meet the EU Cyber Resilience Act. The talk walks through what the Act asks for in this area, including a coordinated disclosure policy, a structured handling process, machine-readable security policies, and optional programs such as bug bounties. It explains why existing material was judged a poor fit: paid ISO standards, enterprise-focused BSI and federal agency guidance, and non-prescriptive guides from OpenSSF and OWASP that cannot show compliance on their own.

The working group set five goals for its text: keep it short enough for the smallest projects, reuse community practices that already work, stay consistent with the Act, tailor it to open source while remaining usable by companies, and publish it under an open source license. The roughly two-page draft lists a small number of mandatory points, such as having a handling process, offering a reporting method that does not require a separate account, following coordinated disclosure, linking to the reporting policy, naming who handles vulnerabilities, reporting to upstream projects, and publishing resolved vulnerabilities. Detailed procedures are left to linked external guidelines rather than prescribed tools.

The draft is hosted on GitHub, where anyone can open issues or pull requests, and a release candidate is targeted for April. The authors intend the result as an input to the European Commission's guidance and attestation work and to European standards bodies. In the questions, the speakers said only harmonized standards carry formal weight under the Act, so the Commission is expected to issue guidance rather than endorse a document directly. Tooling to track compliance was described as outside the group's scope, with other consortia working on it. The practical takeaway is that projects can review and comment on the draft now.

talks.title: UC2 Risk Ruler for CVSS 4.0: Visualizing Vulnerability Severity and Data Confidence
talks.teaser: Explains a visual method for showing how precise and mature a CVSS 4.0 score is, to aid risk decisions.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the UC2 Risk Ruler for CVSS, a visual companion to CVSS 4.0 numeric scores, built by a cyber risk management practitioner who volunteers on the CVSS SIG. Its goal is to show the precision, confidence and maturity behind a score so non-specialists can discuss vulnerabilities more transparently. The speaker reviews the four metric groups: base, threat, environmental and supplemental. Vendors set base metrics from their own view, while consumers add threat and environmental context.

The ruler reads from the bottom up through maturity levels: no CVSS score, a base-metric range, five qualitative bins, eleven whole-number buckets, and finally the precise score. A fictitious vulnerability with a vendor base score of 8.6 falls to 4.2 once threat and environmental metrics are added. At base level the range spans the high band and touches the median, while at the higher level it sits firmly in the four band. The speaker stops there rather than adding supplemental metrics, and notes the ruler can feed quantitative models.

In the question round, the speaker said the ruler does not automate scoring, though the group is working on guidance for ingesting threat intelligence. Its main use is communication, such as explaining to an auditor why an 8.6 may be far lower in a well-defended environment, and it helps justify spending on richer scoring. Asked about vendors that attach their own severity labels, the speaker argued that publishing a range with a score gives customers transparency and shifts responsibility for their deployment to them.

talks.title: Updates from the CVSS SIG
talks.teaser: Reports on CVSS version 4 adoption, new scoring examples, a community survey, and what changes come next.
talks.summary:
The talk is a progress report from the CVSS Special Interest Group, given by co-chair Nick Leali. He describes how adoption of CVSS version 4 has grown over the past year. The CVE program and NVD both added tooling for version 4, the CVE program holds roughly 5,000 version 4 vectors, and GitHub is the largest producer with about 8,000 across reviewed and unreviewed records. Around 56 vendors now publish version 4 scores.

Documentation work continued with new examples covering server-side request forgery, cross-site request forgery, a regression flaw, subsequent system impacts, and cross-site scripting. More FAQ entries were added, many about the scoring math. The speaker also covered vector reassessment, where a vendor takes an existing CVE assessment and produces a vector suited to its own platform. Audience members questioned whether this weakens standardisation and how customers might respond to a vendor score that is lower than the national database score. The speaker stressed that the standard itself is unchanged and that the per-platform assessment is context-based.

The SIG ran a survey in 2024 that drew more than 500 responses. About 74% of respondents viewed version 4 favourably, and most adopters thought it was worth the move. Many organisations combine CVSS with SSVC, EPSS, vendor-supplied scores and internal systems. No new standard is planned soon, with a possible 4.1 update perhaps in 2026, and an enhanced user guide is being prepared for vulnerability management programmes. The speaker warned that version 4 is not a drop-in replacement, so scores will shift and teams should test against their own data.

talks.title: CVSS v4.0 By The Numbers
talks.teaser: Compares CVSS version 3.1 and 4.0 scores across Cisco, CVE, and GitHub data to show how severity ratings shift.
talks.summary:
Nick Leali, a CVSS SIG co-chair and Cisco incident manager, examines how the math in CVSS version 4.0 differs from version 3.1 and why that matters for patch priorities, advisories and compliance. He built a small Python and NumPy script that compares paired scores from several data sets, measuring record counts, average and most common score changes, and how often a score crosses a qualitative rating boundary.

Cisco's own public CVEs showed an average rise of 0.36, with about 15% changing rating band, including a few that dropped from critical to medium. Across 3,516 CVE program records, the average change was 0.19, but roughly a third moved to a different band, creating 491 new medium-rated items. GitHub's reviewed advisories, 2,720 records, skewed toward more high and critical ratings, while its unreviewed set of about 3,400 records saw 33% of boundaries shift.

The second half covered SIG updates and a survey of more than 500 respondents, where 74% said version 4 was worth adopting, though most users combine CVSS with other scoring systems. The takeaway is to avoid ranking by base score alone, to use the full vector with threat and environmental metrics, and for vendors to document when their own ratings deviate from the standard.

talks.title: Vulnrichment: Year One
talks.teaser: Reviews CISA's first year of Vulnrichment, enriching public CVE records with scoring data, and the lessons from its CPE experiment.
talks.summary:
CISA's vulnerability management team presents the first year of Vulnrichment, a project that adds analysis to public CVE records. The speaker explains that CISA already scores vulnerabilities internally with SSVC and maintains the KEV catalog, and Vulnrichment makes that work available. Enrichment is added as an ADP container alongside the CNA's own data. It fills gaps rather than auditing what the CNA published, inheriting KEV flags and adding CVSS, CWE and reference links where they are missing. The work is run in a public GitHub repository.

The middle of the talk covers an experiment with CPE, run from April to December 2024. Choosing a CPE name meant checking dictionaries and working out who owns a product name, which consumed much of the team's time. CISA stopped and refocused on technical vulnerability analysis and faster coverage of new CVEs. The speaker also reviewed public issues and pull requests, reporting an average of 2.1 comments per item and about six and a half days open. One example involved a curl maintainer who disputed a published score on a Sunday; the team fixed it within hours.

The closing takeaways stress transparency, deferring to the CNA when sources disagree, and avoiding long scoring debates. The speaker argues that third-party enrichment raises cost and lowers quality, so originating vendors should supply CVSS and CWE when a record is created. The team plans to keep experimenting, and the talk ends by noting that global software identity remains an unsolved problem.

talks.title: CPE Metadata: Know IT ALL
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of CPE Metadata: Know IT ALL.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, an InfoSec engineer at MongoDB specializing in product security, bug bounty, and CVE disclosures explores the critical role of Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) metadata in vulnerability management. The speaker addresses the fallout from the National Vulnerability Database's (NVD) early 2024 slowdown in enriching Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) with metadata such as Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) scores and CPEs. To ensure vulnerability scanners and automated tools function reliably, the speaker argues that CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) must proactively self-enrich their CVE publications by including CPE metadata at the source.

### Key Topics
- **CVE and Metadata Basics**: The speaker structures CVE data around the "who, what, where, and how" framework: CVE is the vulnerability (who), CVSS score reflects severity (what), CPE pinpoints the affected product and version (where), and CWE outlines the underlying flaw (how).
- **The NVD Enrichment Slowdown**: Historically, industry vulnerability scanners have heavily relied on NVD analysts to populate CVSS and CPE metadata into the NVD CPE dictionary. In early 2024, NVD announced a slowdown in enriching CVEs, creating risks of delayed metadata, vulnerability miscategorization, and unprotected systems.
- **The Gap in CPE Inclusion**: While CNAs publish CVEs via the CVE program's JSON schema, they are not mandated to provide metadata. Historically, over 50% of CVEs contain CVSS and CWE, but only 13.3% of all issued CVEs have ever included CPEs. While CPE inclusion in CVE JSON files hovered at or below 10% historically, it surged to 26% in 2023 and 54% in 2024, partially prompted by NVD's slowdown.
- **CNA Demographics and Adoption**: CVE issuance has grown rapidly, jumping 38% in 2024 after an earlier doubling in 2017. CNA membership reached 447 organizations by 2025. While 288 CNAs (64%) have issued CVEs containing CPEs, manual labor constraints and third-party CVE assignments cause substantial inconsistency across published records.

### Technical Details
- **JSON Schema Structure**: The CVE JSON format accommodates metadata directly within dedicated blocks. CNAs populate the `cna` container, which features an `affected` section containing a `cpes` array. Authorized Data Publishers (ADPs), such as CISA, populate a separate `adp` container.
- **CPE 2.3 Format Breakdown**: The speaker illustrates a CPE string using MongoDB's Rust driver:
  - Prefix: `cpe:2.3` denotes the CPE specification version.
  - Part: `a` specifies application (contrasting with `o` for operating system or `h` for hardware).
  - Vendor: `mongodb` denotes the vendor name.
  - Product: `rust_driver` identifies the specific software.
  - Version: `0.10.0` isolates the affected version for vulnerability identification and patch assessment.
  - Optional Fields and Wildcards: Subsequent fields (update, edition, language, etc.) use wildcards (`*`) as placeholders, with MongoDB server noted as the target software.
- **Operational Workflow at MongoDB**: MongoDB manages an internal CPE database in a spreadsheet mapped to product releases. When issuing a CVE, the team first searches the NVD CPE dictionary to maintain naming consistency, generating new CPE identifiers for novel products and embedding them directly into the CVE JSON file before publication.

### Takeaways
- **Self-Enrichment Benefits CNAs**: By supplying accurate CPEs and CVSS scores at disclosure, vendors maintain narrative control over their vulnerabilities, eliminate discrepancies between vendor bulletins and third-party databases, and minimize customer confusion.
- **Automation and Scanner Reliability**: Vulnerability scanners depend on standardized product identifiers to pinpoint affected systems. Direct CNA enrichment guarantees scanners can accurately detect vulnerable assets even when central bodies like NVD or CISA experience backlogs.
- **Call to Action**: CNAs are urged to overcome the manual friction of initial setup by systematically integrating CPE metadata into their CVE release workflows, driving enablement and resilience across the vulnerability management ecosystem.

talks.title: Madness of Vulnerability Management in Modern Cloud, Container, How to Win the Battle...
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Madness of Vulnerability Management in Modern Cloud, Container, How to Win the Battle....
talks.summary:
## Overview

This talk addresses how cloud and container technologies have fundamentally transformed vulnerability management from traditional on-premise approaches. The speakers discuss the dramatic increase in vulnerabilities (262,000 CVEs in NVD at time of talk; 40x growth since 2015), the failure of traditional CVSS scoring and SLA-based remediation to address modern complexity, and present a threat-centric framework for prioritizing vulnerabilities.

## The Vulnerability Explosion

Vulnerability numbers have grown exponentially—40x since 2015, with projections reaching 1 million by 2031. Meanwhile, security team budgets grow only 6% annually, creating an impossible gap. Exploitation timelines have compressed dramatically: from 15 days to 3 minutes between CVE disclosure and working exploit. LLMs have accelerated both offense and defense: approximately 50% of new code is now generated via LLMs ("vibe coding"), and attackers can automatically generate working exploits by feeding vulnerability descriptions into ChatGPT. Additionally, attackers are developing GPT-style code scanners and exploit generators, giving them new scale and speed.

## The Complexity Shift-Left Exposed

Traditional vulnerability management in 2015 focused on network scanning and OS patching with simple remediation paths. Cloud adoption and shift-left scanning practices revealed nightmarish complexity: software composition analysis, container vulnerabilities, supply chain dependencies, and multiple deployment paths. A single import statement (e.g., importing a library or LLM SDK) can expose massive attack surface. The industry's response—running multiple scanners at every stage—creates overwhelming noise: the same vulnerability is reported 5-10 times (by code scanners, container scanners, registry scanners, runtime scanners) with no clear remediation path.

## Core Problem: Missing Context and Coordination

The speakers identify that application security and infrastructure/cloud security are treated as separate disciplines, creating gaps. Four foundational elements are missing from most programs:
1. **Attribution**: Who owns this vulnerability/asset?
2. **Lineage**: How does code transform through container images to running deployments?
3. **Traceability**: Which application built this specific container?
4. **Reachability**: Can this vulnerability actually be exploited (at code level, container level, network level, or by known threat actors)?

Containers are the "hinge point" between application and infrastructure security, but organizations rarely coordinate across application security, infrastructure security, and operations teams. The traditional response—dumping all findings into spreadsheets and telling developers to "fix all of this by SLA X, Y, Z"—fails because attackers only need to be right once while developers must be right always.

## Threat-Centric Prioritization Framework

Rather than reporting all discovered vulnerabilities, the speakers propose a layered risk model:
- **CVSS score** (raw severity)
- **Business context** (is the affected application running, and how critical is it?)
- **Reachability analysis** at four levels: code-level loading, container runtime execution, network exposure, and threat actor interest (via CTI)
- **Exploit evidence** (EPSS scoring, CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, threat intelligence)
- **Vulnerability DNA**: Using CWE classification and machine-learning-based reclassification of NVD data, they identify patterns that predict exploitability. Key finding: approximately 40% of ransomware exploits involve vulnerabilities with remote code execution or memory corruption as their threat impact, suggesting these types are inherently more likely to be targeted by threat actors. Zero-day exploits and ransomware campaigns show consistent patterns: remote code execution and memory corruption vulnerabilities are leveraged far more frequently.

This approach dramatically reduces noise: starting with 262,000+ raw vulnerabilities, filtering by exploit availability, reachability analysis, and predicted exploitability yields a tractable subset actually requiring remediation.

## Practical Recommendations

1. **Replace SLA-driven remediation** with risk-based targets. Instead of "fix all critical by SLA," communicate a risk threshold and allow teams to choose remediation strategies (patch, update library, rebuild deployment, decommission application).
2. **Eliminate contextual duplication**: Map duplicate reports of the same vulnerability back to the actual remediation location (source repository or library), rather than asking developers to fix the same issue across multiple scanner reports.
3. **Shift scanning left to registry level**: Scan container images before deployment to prevent vulnerable images from running in the first place.
4. **Coordinate teams intelligently**: Patch teams don't need vulnerability details until a patch exists; network security teams deploy signatures for temporary mitigation; development teams fix the source. Provide each team only actionable information relevant to their role.
5. **Use proven risk formulas**: Risk = likelihood × impact. Populate likelihood with cloud-specific factors (reachability, threat actor activity), and impact with business context (application criticality).

## Key Takeaways

Modern vulnerability management cannot treat application and infrastructure security as separate. It requires unified asset ownership, traceability through the entire software pipeline, and cross-team coordination. Traditional CVSS-centric scoring and blanket SLAs create false confidence and alert fatigue. A threat-centric approach using exploit evidence, reachability analysis, and vulnerability DNA classification allows security teams to focus remediation where it actually reduces business risk. The core insight: don't report more vulnerabilities—report fewer, but more accurate ones, to the right teams, at the right time.

talks.summary:
The speaker, who works with the Open Source Security Foundation, walks product security teams through the EU Cyber Resilience Act. He stresses that he is not a lawyer and presents the law as consumer protection for products with digital elements sold into the European Union, with penalties that can reach a share of annual revenue. Many of its requirements codify practices that security teams already use, such as secure development and vulnerability management.

The middle of the talk covers the Annex I obligations. These include producing an SBOM on request, a support period of at least five years, security updates kept available for ten years and provided free of charge, and sharing fixes with upstream projects. For actively exploited vulnerabilities, he outlines an early warning within 24 hours, an advisory with fixes or workarounds within 72 hours, and a final report about 14 days later. Audience questions on usage fees, embargoes and software-as-a-service scope were mostly answered with advice to consult legal counsel.

He closes with practical steps: work out which product class applies, name a national CSIRT contact, set up a single point of contact and disclosure policy, and engage with upstream projects. He cites Linux Foundation research showing low awareness of the law, and a security baseline that maps to 19 of the 21 Annex I items. Several details are still being standardised, so teams should track the European Commission and the standards bodies.

Scanner vendors, CNAs, and NVD stakeholders debate whether CNA CVE JSON should be canonical, why enrichments diverge, and how ADP containers might let each vendor state relevance without rewriting upstream records. Oracle and Cisco voices add ontology, alias mapping, SBOM ingestion gaps, and parent-child dependency chains.

Practitioners should expect identifier politics to dominate real risk decisions until records mandate complete product metadata, shared definitions for component versus application, and consumption of vendor VEX. Near-term outcomes emphasized include rapid CPE extension, official PURL in CVE records, quality-working-group guidance for smaller CNAs, and clearer rules for authoritative naming rather than another greenfield identifier reset.

talks.summary:
### Overview
This panel discussion, titled 'Software Identity in the Vulnerability Management Ecosystem', explores the challenges and ongoing efforts surrounding software identification standards within vulnerability management, specifically regarding the CVE and NVD ecosystems. Moderated by Alex Hmers (MITRE CVE and CWE project lead), the panel features Megazone (F5, co-chair of the CVE Quality Working Group), Chris Turner (NVD/NIST senior adviser), Steve Springett (ServiceNow, CycloneDX and ECMA TC54 chair), and Andrew (MITRE, Omnibore project). The session levels on the premise that no single identifier currently addresses every software identification need, necessitating a multi-identifier ecosystem spanning centralized, federated, and decentralized schemes.

### Key Topics
- **The Multi-Identifier Ecosystem**: The panel discusses the necessity of accommodating different identifier formats rather than mandating a single solution, comparing centralized, defined systems against decentralized and inherent models.
- **CPE in the CVE Record Format**: Recent updates added structured support for Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) applicability language in the CVE record schema, addressing prior shortcomings where CPE was simply an ambiguous array of values.
- **Package URL (purl)**: Originating as an open specification started around 2016–2017, purl provides decentralized identification aligned with package managers (e.g., npm, PyPI, Maven) and is pursuing standardization under ECMA TC54.
- **Omnibore**: A newer, completely distributed scheme producing inherent identifiers (artifact IDs) derived directly from binary or source artifacts rather than centralized names or package registries.
- **CVE Record Integration and Proposals**: Active proposals in the CVE Quality Working Group seek to expand software identity options by introducing generic identifier support alongside dedicated additions for purl and Omnibore.
- **Authority and Ecosystem Governance**: The panel addresses whether CNAs should be mandated to provide identifiers, the role of Authorized Data Publishers (ADPs) in enriching records, and handling downstream vendor impacts.

### Technical Details
- **Defined vs. Inherent Identifiers**: Citing CISA's software identification ecosystem option analysis taxonomy, the panel contrasts defined identifiers (which depend on a central dictionary or list, such as CPE or purl's types list) with inherent identifiers like Omnibore, which are derived deterministically from the artifact itself.
- **Identifier Granularity Funnel**: Steve Springett describes an identifier funnel where CPE operates at the broad product level at the top, purl operates in the middle at the package level, and Omnibore operates at the bottom for precise artifact-level tracking.
- **Version Constraints and Ranges**: Addressing concerns about purl lacking native version range matching in vulnerability contexts, panelists explain that CVE record proposals separate the package identifier from version constraint fields—reusing the CPE range model (e.g., starting/ending version bounds) rather than requiring multiple explicit purls.
- **Non-Package-Manager and Commercial Software**: For software outside traditional package registries (such as C/C++ or commercial software), purl supports extensible types like GitHub/Bitbucket or the SWID purl type, which adapts ISO SWID tag attributes into a decentralized package URL.
- **CPE Modernization and Scaling**: CPE 2.3 faces challenges scaling across tens of thousands of product iterations. NVD is working toward modernizing CPE serialization from XML to JSON and exploring expanded automated tooling.

### Takeaways
- **A Multi-Identifier Future is Inevitable**: Industry participants and standards bodies recognize that different layers of the software supply chain require different identification granularities—from products (CPE) to packages (purl) to binaries/artifacts (Omnibore).
- **Support over Mandates**: The CVE program focuses on enabling industry-standard identifiers within CVE records rather than dictating a mandatory standard, avoiding insurmountable barriers for participating CNAs.
- **Evolving Community Standards**: Both purl (via ECMA TC54) and Omnibore are actively developing open specifications, implementations, and cross-reference mappings, while NVD continues working on modernization and tooling improvements.

talks.teaser: Explains how Belgium's federal government ran a live bug-bounty event under a new safe harbor law.
talks.summary:
Susan Bush, who managed the project, explains how Belgium's Centre for Cyber Security Belgium (CCB) organised Hack the Government in 2024, the first event of its kind in the country. She traces the path that led there, starting with a 2014 case in which a hacker who reported flaws was criminally charged. That history led to a whistleblower law passed in February 2023 that protects ethical hackers from criminal prosecution if they meet four conditions: no intent to cause harm, prompt reporting, proportionate action, and no disclosure without CCB authorisation.

Community building came next. The CCB sponsored a Belgian hacker conference to showcase the law, collected sign-ups on a typewriter to keep personal data away from digital leaks, and ran the event through a bug bounty platform with a Discord server for coordination. Four federal public services agreed to be targets after months of talks, and their concerns about reputation, confidentiality, extra work and downtime were addressed directly. Participation was capped at 50 Belgian citizens checked by ID, with places split between students and professionals.

Over 15 days the event produced 154 reports, of which 85 were validated, ranging from low to critical. One finding led to a CVE in a security product rated 8.8. talks.teaser: Shows how AI bills of materials track models, datasets and frameworks to expose poisoning and supply chain risks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a hypothetical 2030 case in which a trading firm loses $80 million after a poisoned upstream model reaches production. From there the speaker explains why organizations need to know what went into their AI systems. Models, training datasets and frameworks are pulled from open source much as software dependencies are, yet existing tools such as software composition analysis and vulnerability databases cover them poorly. Risks surveyed include data poisoning, backdoored models, denial of service, model inversion that can expose training data, and prompt injection.

Two real cases anchor the discussion. An NVIDIA patch fixed a high-severity flaw in its model-running framework that affects its hardware, and a Zen ML platform API issue allowed access with an existing username and a new password, with no CVE mapping on the NVD at the time. The AI BOM is presented as an extension of the SBOM, supported by CycloneDX and SPDX. Useful fields include model source, versions tracked by commit hash, performance metrics, model and dataset licensing, and data classification. Generating these is hard because model cards are free-form text, so the working group is preparing an open source generator.

Answering a question about data-driven versus code-driven attacks, the speaker said training data manipulation shapes model behavior directly and should be handled alongside development risks. The closing call to action urges attendees to build AI BOMs for third-party models, run risk assessments using OWASP frameworks, and engage with the CISA-linked working group, which has defined seven priority use cases.

talks.summary:
This session was an open conversation rather than a fixed talk, led by two coordinators from a government agency and a Japanese coordination center. It opened with a problem statement from an international coordinated vulnerability disclosure community of practice: members hold different pictures of what disclosure covers, so information can fail to reach the people who need it. The audience was polled on years of disclosure experience, CNA status and CVE data use, then invited to describe cases that went wrong.

Several contributions illustrated the difficulties. A telecom security lead described building an ad hoc route for researchers who wanted payment, using a third party that verified identity, before any formal process existed. Bug bounty programs drew sharp disagreement. One speaker said a public program launched without thorough testing had cost a former employer $2.5 million in one month, and described a maturity path from authenticated pentesting to private bounty and only then public bounty. Others saw bounties as a way to bring fresh eyes to high-priority products. Cross-border concerns came up too: vendors said national partners sometimes received reports late, and a shared portal made direct notification between parties hard. Suggested fixes included machine-readable advisories, a state-machine protocol for tracking disclosure, and limiting pre-disclosure to parties with a clear need to know. A historical case involving a widely used DNS project showed how a global group coordinated a patch while its maintainer was unreachable.

The closing discussion covered coordinators training inexperienced researchers through a first case, then stepping back. Speakers stressed that finding the right vendor contact is difficult, that security.txt and DNS records can help, and that communication should focus on risk rather than patch status. The main takeaway was that relationships across the community matter most, so practitioners were encouraged to join existing groups and keep talking after the session.

talks.summary:
This talk looks at product security incident response at a large software-as-a-service vendor, drawn from the speaker's experience running a product security response team. The speaker argues that hosted products carry different problems from on-premises software. Customer instances sit on the internet and are easy to discover, and researchers can begin testing web applications with little more than a browser. Because the network attack vector pushes severity scores up, the stakes feel high. Shared responsibility also means customers sometimes have to act quickly, and the vendor often has no visibility into customer traffic.

The middle of the talk covers hard trade-offs. Rate limiting or a web firewall can break automated customer jobs, and forced changes or blocked rollbacks can cause outages of their own. Disclosure timing is debated: some want a patch window before full details are published, while others wait for customer tooling to flag the issue. Customer security contacts go stale, and implementation partners may never receive notices. On the opportunity side, the speaker suggested using telemetry, scanning activity and version adoption data to decide what to fix first, and treating demo instances as an early warning signal.

In the question round, the speaker described reviewing disclosures for technical accuracy, checking whether third-party CVEs affect the product by testing their preconditions, and advised a company in transformation to consider splitting CERT and product security work as it grows. The takeaway is that SaaS vendors must weigh disruption, precedent and the amount of customer action required when deciding how and when to disclose.

They emphasize maturity, scalability, and sustainability pillars, stakeholder rolodexes, splitting CERT from PSIRT to end resource conflicts, and mapping discovery through disclosure onto a high-traffic bug bounty with HackerOne intake, SLA tracking, blameless engineering loops, and researcher outreach. Jeff walks discovery, triage, remediation, and coordinated disclosure habits—including documenting lessons and managing rising AI-report noise—while Sarah notes audit wins from shared industry language. talks.teaser: Explains why vulnerability management is harder in operational technology, from NERC CIP patch deadlines to legacy systems.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why vulnerability management is harder in operational technology (OT) than in IT. The speakers define OT and industrial control systems and show how they overlap with critical infrastructure sectors. They argue that reliability, safety and performance come first in these environments, so availability limits shape every patching decision, and that compliance and security are related but not the same goal.

The middle of the talk focuses on NERC CIP-007 R2, the patch management requirement, which the speakers describe as one of the most commonly violated standards. Its timeline gives 35 calendar days to evaluate a security patch and then 35 more days to apply it or document a mitigation plan. They describe how incomplete asset inventories, legacy systems such as Windows XP and NT still running critical functions, and geographically spread substations with short outage windows make manual patching slow. They also point to weak vulnerability data, including missing or outdated CPE entries, and to screenshots of vendor advisories being used as compliance evidence.

The speakers close by urging vendors to publish security advisories in a machine-readable JSON format so that automation becomes possible. In the question period, one example describes a worm found on an air-gapped network running Windows XP. Their advice for practitioners is to rely on segmentation, access restriction and other compensating controls when no patch exists, and to work closely with vendors.

talks.title: Validating Vulnerability Analysis with Statistical Analysis of Metadata
talks.teaser: Shows how clustering CVSS, CWE and component metadata can check impact ratings and flag unusual vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Vulnerability reports keep growing while analyst headcount stays roughly flat, so each analyst handles more flaws. Red Hat's team asked whether vulnerability metadata can help assign impact faster. They used three inputs as independent variables: CVSS, CWE and affected component, with the four-level impact rating as the outcome. Keith Grant explained how each field was turned into an ordered numeric space so that similar flaws sit near each other.

Alexander Bushkin then presented clustering over 7,415 flaws from four years of data, after restricting to consistent weakness views and noting skew from a surge of kernel reports. Bands were named by their dominant confidentiality, integrity and availability pattern. The lowest band was mostly availability loss, where a memory-leak weakness was the most common CWE. Another band showed mainly low confidentiality impact, and a higher one centred on data manipulation, where a weakness about mishandling extra input values can lead to memory overwrites and code execution.

The talk closed with an outlier check: the only critical flaw in one band was confirmed as correct, since it had high integrity and availability impact with no confidentiality impact. The practical idea is to show analysts the nearest neighbouring flaws while they edit metadata, so they can spot likely mislabelling or unusual cases without flattening every flaw into its neighbours. The team plans to refine search methods and how chained weaknesses are handled.

talks.title: The Enriched CVE Record: Redefining Completeness and Quality for Greater Impact
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Enriched CVE Record: Redefining Completeness and Quality for Greater Impact.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Alex Summers, MITRE's CVE and CWE project lead, discusses the evolution of CVE data enrichment and how expectations around CVE record completeness have transformed. Originally defined in 1999 by just three core elements—an ID, a brief description, and an external reference—CVE records now require far more contextual metadata to support modern vulnerability management. Summers highlights how the CVE Program has transitioned from centralized authoring by MITRE to a federated model empowering CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) to supply critical enrichment data directly at the time of disclosure.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Record Completeness:** Historical definitions of CVE completeness versus modern expectations, where security consumers demand metrics like CVSS severity scores, CWE weakness types, and software identification.
- **Centralization vs. Federation:** Prior to 2016, MITRE authoring every CVE did not scale. Federation to CNAs has enabled broader coverage and timely reporting.
- **The Enrichment Initiative & Tooling:** Launched in April 2024, the CVE Program's enrichment initiative urged CNAs to enrich their own records. This effort was significantly aided by community tooling like Vulnogram, which lowered barriers to adding structured enrichment.
- **Enrichment Recognition List (ERL):** Introduced in September to acknowledge CNAs routinely providing CVSS and CWE data, tracked and published on a bi-weekly cadence to incentivize adoption.
- **Third-Party Enrichment and Backlogs:** Historical reliance on third parties like NVD or current efforts like CISA's Authorized Data Publisher (ADP) / Vulnrichment, especially during lulls in downstream processing.

### Technical Details
- **Historical Baseline:** In 1999, a CVE record required only an ID, description, and external reference (a format preserved on legacy servers for 1999 advisories).
- **Enrichment Metadata:** Today's ecosystem depends on standards like CVSS, CWE, software identifiers (CPE, package URLs), EPSS, and KEV catalog entries for operational prioritization.
- **Structured Format & CNA Authority:** Program format updates (developed with the Quality Working Group) allow CNAs—the authoritative source who understand their own products best—to embed CVSS, CWE, and CPE metadata at disclosure rather than waiting for third-party analysis.
- **ERL Implementation:** Evaluates active CNAs within specific timeframes (e.g., checking data within a four-week window of their most recent record across a year), showing CNA participation rising into the 70% range.

### Takeaways & Discussion
Summers emphasizes that enriching records at disclosure provides defenders with timely, accurate data and avoids downstream delays. During the Q&A, Summers addressed practical challenges: MITRE's CNA of Last Resort (CNA-LR) struggles to enrich records because researchers often lack developer-level insights; discrepancies raised by attendees regarding ERL inclusion counts and publishing timeframes; and the clarification that MITRE acts as secretariat and root rather than a centralized auditing body for CNA data quality. While third parties like CISA ADP and NVD provide secondary enrichment queues, CNAs remain the primary target for driving data completeness.

talks.title: Vulnerability Root Cause Mapping with CWE
talks.teaser: Explains how grounded LLMs and retrieval can map CVE records to CWE root causes, with cost and accuracy figures.
talks.summary:
Root cause mapping links a CVE record to the CWE weakness behind it, which supports disclosure, vulnerability management and feedback into design. The speakers argue that the quality of CVE input data largely decides how good any mapping can be. Chris Madden walks through an LLM pipeline built on grounding: enrich each CVE with key phrases, reference summaries and consensus mappings, then use keyword, semantic and graph-based retrievers to narrow about a thousand CWEs to a short list of roughly ten before a model picks one or two.

In a run over about 7,000 records from a Top 25 review set, the pipeline cost around $15 in model usage plus about $2 for embeddings. Its output matched the expert CWE exactly in about 81% of cases and landed within two steps in the CWE graph in roughly 90%. Abstraction levels agreed well. Misses clustered around access control wording and records whose reference links could not be crawled, and when a record offered too little evidence the model said so instead of guessing. A three-agent analyzer, critic and resolver setup added cost without improving results.

The main takeaway is that complete, accurate and timely CVE data at the point of entry matters most. Presenters recommend that LLMs offer a short list with rationale and confidence for a subject matter expert to accept or refine, and that newly published CWEs be handled by updating the retrieval corpus rather than fine-tuning. They also propose a shared benchmark data set so that academic and industry tools can be compared, and they invite community input on it and on a planned CWE chatbot.

talks.title: Practical Software Bill of Materials: From Generation to Distribution Workshop
talks.teaser: Walks through generating, enriching, signing and distributing SBOMs with open-source tools such as Syft, Trivy and Cosign.
talks.summary:
The workshop follows the life cycle of a software bill of materials, from first generation to distribution and everyday use. The presenters start with SBOMs produced by Trivy and a kubectl scan, which lack basics such as author, supplier, repository and license details. They add top-level document and component metadata with an augmentation tool, then enrich components from package data sources so that documentation links, licenses and release dates appear.

Verification comes next. Using sbomqs, the presenters show quality scores improving, with components listing a supplier rising from none to about 2,000 of roughly 4,000. They note that intermediate build components often trace to no open-source package, so the producer must fill those gaps. The SBOM is then signed as a detached signature with a certificate through Cosign, and separately wrapped as the predicate of an attestation, and both forms are bundled into a single JSON Lines file.

For distribution, the talk covers GitHub releases, OCI registries, attestation stores and bomctl, which fetches linked SBOMs recursively and pushes them elsewhere. The final section covers operations: loading SBOMs into GUAC over time, correlating them with OSV vulnerability data, and checking which products are affected when a new advisory appears. Attendees leave with practical advice: add metadata, verify signer identity, and never send SBOMs by email.

The talk starts with the speaker's first visit to the annual conference in 2014 and how open the community felt to a newcomer. FIRST helps members quickly find the right contacts during an incident, gives access to technical material, and lets teams share practices that prevent and respond to threats.

The middle of the talk covers FIRST's collaboration forums. The speaker points to the annual National CSIRTs meeting, which the SEI hosts alongside the conference, as an invitation-only space where teams with national responsibilities can discuss problems specific to them. The chair also stresses that members from every region should have ways to contribute, so that programs reflect challenges seen worldwide. Communication and collaboration skills are presented as equally important to technical ability, since they help members write standards together and explain technical issues to policy makers.

The closing section looks ahead to the board's shift from operational to strategic governance, which is meant to grow programs and strengthen local and regional community building. The advice for emerging professionals is to build professional relationships alongside technical skills, because those connections matter during critical incidents. Joining FIRST is framed as taking a place in a worldwide network focused on a safer internet.

For downstream users, they suggest checking what an upstream project can and cannot do, subscribing to release and security mailing lists, and using tools such as OpenSSF Scorecard, OSV, VEX statements and Sigstore to watch for signals. The closing advice is to be an informed open source consumer, even for maintainers who depend on other people's code, and to establish contacts before an incident happens.
